THE SNOWDROP. Pale, fragile flower, with drooping head, How humble thou, though beautiful ; Companion of the winter snows, Adorning garden, field, and dell. Dust thou not fear to bloom alone, In this thy spotle.s bed of snow. 'hy gay companions, all have gone, When wintry winds begin to blow. How desolate all nature seems. The naked tree , and shrubs, and bowers; All frozen, a. e the limpid streams:— The beasts, in coverts, shivering cowers. The cold, bleak wind .1 winter sighs, 'mos Through leafless trees, a sad refrain, The frost king, with his icy touch, Binds nature's scenes with frescoed chain. The birds have left their shady bowers, No more we hear their thrilling chimes. • They've gone to sport. 'neath sunny skies, And sing their songs In other climes. Amid these dreary winter scenes. Like thee, fair flower. I'm all alone; The one who made life sweet to me, A I To other scenes afar, has gone. But soon the bright, glad, sunny spring,. Will come with an her lovely train, t The flowers, the birds, the foliage green And bring my dear one back again. Bt. Helens. .1. G. Pima/wont., A DEWDROP. I dreamed that my soul was a dewdrop. As a dewdrop I fell to the ground; • And here, in the hearts of the flowers. A grave of sweet odour I found : But my sisters, the other drops, drew me, With them in a silvery throng, To their sweet source, dancing round me. And, drawing me, danced me along. Where my sisters and I went dancing, NEI Gay flowers on the green banks grew; And the flowers I kiss'd, and with kisses ;KC greeted the gold sand too ; Will down, with the brooklet, I bounded, On tie wheel of the water-mill, And whirl'd it; and wander'cl, and water'd The thirsty young corn on the hill. Thence over the hill-top headlong. As I fell to the hollows below, "Here," I thought, "is the end of my journey. And my life, too, is ended now." But the current drew me and drew me on, By forest, and dale, and down, And under the turrets and bridges. . And into the roaring town. Onward, and onward, and never Any moment of perfect bliss, And, with lips that sought love everlasting I snatch'd but a fleeting kiss. Onward, and onward, till falling Into the infinite main, In its fathomless waters I buried My love, and my hope, and pain. And "here," I thought, "all ends surely," As the great billow bore me away, "Here my spirit shall rest, and for ever. From its longing, and labour, and play." -.But anew to the azure of heaven Was my being unborne ; and anew soindo ' Prom the heaven to the earth I descended In a drop of celestial dew. No chain is stronger than its weakest link. Spiritually, ma man is stronger than his weakest act. "Clara," asked Tom, "what animal dropped from the clouds ?"—" The rain, dear," was the reply. Every man has three characters ; that which he exhibits, that which he has, and thai which be thinks he has. The speaker who divides his discourse into too many 'heads will find it difficult to get attentive ears to all of them. The number of one-armed young men seen driving out with young ladies these summer evenings is truly appalling. An old soldier at our elbow says that one arm is invariably lost during an engagement. "How came you to fail in your examination?" asked the ;tutor, "I thought I crammed you thoroughly." ('Well, you see," replied the student, "the fact was you crammed me so tight I couldn't get it out." THE CENSUS.—The following conversation relative to the taking of the census was overheard at Gateshead :—Tom: " Aa see they're gan te tyek the census agyen, Jack." Jack : "Aye, man: wey, non, they'll get varra little sense ot of than, fool Life is made of little things. It is the little duties that make up the business of the day, the little words of cheer, the little acts of kindnese that spread sunshine around our path. The absence of these makes the chill of winter in the heart and in the home. The superinieildent of a Sunday school asked the scholars .—" With what remarkable weapon did Samson at one time slay a number of Philistines ?"—For a while there was no answer, and the superintendent, to assist the children a. little, began tapping his jaw with.the tip of his finger, at the same tkne saying—" What's this, what's this to . which a little fellow innocently replied, " The jawbone of an ass, sir." - QUESTION'S FOR FARIIERS.—A brilliant correspondent of the Putnim Patriot, who evidently cares little for agricul- tural mitters, suggests the following themes for discussion by the Farmers' Club of Pomfret :—Why* do not cows sit -dawn to rest the same as dogs? Why does a dog turn round a few times before he lies down? Why does a cow get up from the ground hind end first, and a horse fore end first? Why thee a squirrel come down a tree head first, and a cat tail-first? Why does a mule kick with its hind foot, and a sheep with its fore foot? 4.• NEWBPAPER WONDER.—The Railway Journal, an American newspaper, containing the latest intelligence with respect to home and foreign politics, the money-market, Congress debates, and theatrical events is now printed and published daily in the trains...running between New York and San Francisco. All the news with which its columns are filled is telegraphed from different parts of the States to certain statidns on the line, them collected by the editorial staff travelling in the train, and set up, printed, and cir- culated among the subscribing passengers, -while the iron horse is persistently traversing plains and valleys, crossing rivers, and ascending mountain ranges. Every morning the traveller may have his newspaper served up with his coffee, and thus keep himself informed of all that is going on in the wide world during a seven days' journey covering over three thousand miles of ground. He who pays his sub- scription at New York, which he can do at the railway ticket-office, receives the last copy of his paper on the sum- snit of the Sierra Nevada. The production of a news-sheet from a flying printing-office at an elevation of some ten thousand feet above the level of the sea is most assuredly a performance worthy of conspicuous record in journalistic annals and highly creditable to American enterprise. A Boss LIAR.—He looked a bit hard up, but he had a pleasant face and smooth address, as he walked into the office of a railroad running West and asked for the super- intendents. When conducted to that officer's desk, be be- gan :—" I want the favour of a pass to Buffalo." "Can't haV it," was the prompt reply. e' I expected that answer, and am prepared for it. I did not come here with a tale of woe. I have not been robbed." "No ?" "Not a rob. I did not lose my money on the street. I arm not obliged to rash home to see my wife die. lam not a consumptive who is anxious to get home and die among his friends. All these pleas are old" "Yes, very old and thin." a And yet I want a pass to Buffalo. I feel that I have a right to aek it." "On what grounds?" "This morning leaved the life of a passenger on one of your transfer boats. He was a big, red-whiskered man named Clark. Had he gone over- board, it would have cost you perhaps 50,000 dols, to settle the claim." "Clark? Big man with red whiskers? Wretched man, you know not what you did? That's the man who has already got a claim for 20,000 dols. against us for breaking his leg. If von had • only let him go over- board, we could have settled with his heirs for less than a quarter of the amount. Go out—go away. You have taken thousands of dollars out of our pockets by your med- dlesome act." The beat walked out without a word, but as he reachr2d the door he was heard to grumble: "I thought J was the best liar on the Atlantic emit, but I might as well hang up from this deal."— Wall Street News. CARLYLE: AND THE DUICE or WELLINOTON.—" One even' lug, i at Bath House, I saw her (Mrs. Carlyle) n a grand soirée softly step up and (unnoticed, as she thought, by anybody) kiss the old Duke of Wellingtonis shoulder. That, perhaps, was one of the prettiest thingsever saw there. Duke was then very old, and hitched languidly' about, hich rspeaking only when spoken to, some "w-w" C's Garter perhaps had very little meaning in it ; he had on his der, his gold-buckle stock, and was very clean and trim ; but, except making appearance at certain evening parties, half an hour in each, perhaps hardly knew what he was doing. From Bath House we saw his funeral procession a while alter ; and, to our disgust, in one of the mourning coaches, some official or dignitary reading a newspaper. The hearse (seventeen tons of bronze), the arrangements generally, were vulgar and disgusting ' • but the fact itself impressed everybody; the street rows all silently doffed bat as the body passed; and London, altogether, seemed to be holding its breath. A dim, almost wet kind of day ; adieu, adieu. With Wellington I don't think either of us had ever spoken; though we both esteemed him heartily. I had known his face for nearly thirty years ; he also, I think, ' had grown to know mine, as that of somebody who wished him well ; not otherwise, I dare„say, or the proprietor's name at all ; but I have seen him gaze at me a little as we passed on the streets. To speak to him with my notions of his ways of thinking, and his articulate endowments, was net among my longings. I went once to the House 4.1 Lords especially to hear the sound of his voice, and 80 complete my little private physiognomical portrait of him ; a fine aquiline voice I found it, quite like the face of him; and got a great Instruction and lesson, which has stayed with me, out of his ittle speech itself (Lord Ellenborough's "Gates of Som- nauth " the subject, about which I cared nothing) ; speech of the most haggly, hawky, pinched, and meagre kind, so ar as utterance and eloquence went; but potent for convic- on beyond any other; nay, I may say, quite exclusively if all 8-Ahem that night, which were mere 'melodious wind' to rde (Brougham's, Derby's, dm.), while this hitching, stunted, hogging discourse of ten or thirteen minutes had ' made the duke's opinion completely mine too. I thought of Oliver Cromwell withal, and have often since, oftener than ever before, said to myself,' Is not this (to make your opinion mine) the aim of all 'eloquence,' rhetoric, and Demosthe ale artillery practice ? And what is it good for ? F ads ! get a true insight and belief of your own as te the er ; th it is the way to get your belief into me, end it the only way t"—Mr. Carlyle's Reminiscences.

IL SATURDAY, MARI WILD BIRDS PROTECTION ACT. The Wild Birds Protection Act (1880) came into force on the 2nd inst. As many of our readers will doubtless be interested in the matter, we reprint the two more important sections of the Act, together with the schedule:—
lAN
Ts. it i,

- ------- -- -- - 3. Any person who between the first day of March and the first day of August in any year after the passing of this Act shall knowingly and:wilfully shoot, or attempt to shoot, or shall use any boat for the purpose of shooting or causing to be shot, any wild bird, or shall use any lime, trap, snare, net, or other instrument for the purpose of taking any wild bird, or shall expose or offer for sale, or shall have in his control oil possession after the fifteenth day of. March, any wild bird recently killed or taken, shall, on conviction of any such offence before any two Justices of the Peace in Eng- land and Wales or Ireland, or before the Sheriff in Scotland, in the case of any wild bird which is included in the sche- dule hereunto annexed, forfeit and pay for every such bird in respect of which an offence has been committed a sum not exceeding one pound, and, in the case of any other wild bird, shall for a first offence be reprimanded and discharged on payment of costs, and for every subsequent offence for- feit and pay for every such wild bird in respect of which is an offence committed a sum of money not exceeding five shillings, in addition to the costs, unless such person shall prove that the said wild bird was either killed or taken or bought or received during the period in which such wild bird couli be legally killed or taken, or from some person residing out of the United Kingdom. This section shall not apply to the owner or occupier of any land or to any person authorised by the owner or occupier of any land, killing or taking any wild bird on such land not included in the sche- dule hereto annexed. 4. Where any person shall be found offending against this Act, it . shall be lawful for any person to require the person so offending to give his Christian name, surname, and place of abode, and in case the person so offending shall after being so required, refuse to give his real name or place of abode, or give an untrue name or 'place of abode, he shall be liable on being convicted of any such offence to for- feit and pay, in addition to the penalties imposed by Sec- tion three, such sum of money not exceeding ten shillings sterling as to the justices or sheriff shall seem meet. The following is the schedule detailing the birds protected by the Act : American Quail Kittiwake Sea Lark Auk Lapwing Sea-mew Averet Loon Sea Parrot Bee-eater Mallard Sea Swallow Bittern Marrot Shearwater Bonxie Merganser Shell Drake Colin Murre Shoveller Cornish Clough Night-hawk Sims Coulterneb Night-jar Smew Cuckoo Nightingale Snipe Curlew Oriole Bolan Goose Diver Owl ' Spoonbill Dotterell Ox Bird Stint Dunbird Oyster-catcher Stone Curlew Dunlin Peewit Stonehatch Eider Duck Petrel Summer Snipe Fern Owl Phalarope Tarrock Fulmar Plover Teal Gannet Ploverspage Tern Goatsucker Pochard Thick-knee Godwit Puffin Tyst,ey ' Goldfinch Pwere Whaup Grebe Razorbill Whimbrel Greenshank Redshank Widgeon Guillemot Reeve or Ruff Wild Duck Gull (except Black- Roller Willock backed Gull) Sanderling Woodcock Hoopoe Sandpiper Woodpecker Kingfisher Scout
NATIONAL LIBRAIZIES.—The Globe says that, according to statistics lately published in Vienna, it would appear that Austria is better off than any other State in the world for the

means of public instruction. It claims to possess 577 libraries, containing together nearly sfr million volumes, without counting manuscripts, which would give a proportion of nearly 27 volumes for each 100 inhabitants. The nation which comes next to Austria is said to be France, which boasts 500 libraries, containing about 41, million volumes; and this is not surprising when it is considered how well off even the remote towns generally are for public museums and reading-rooms. Italy is not very far behind, with 493 libraries and 4,350,000 volumes; and next Prussia, with above 400 libraries, and above 21 million books. Great Britain is far down in the list, and is reported as having only 200 libraries; but although they are thus only half as numerous as the Prussian, they are allowed to contain nearly a quarter of a million more printed books. If the order of precedence is made out in proportion to the num- ber of inhabitants, it will, as the Austrian statistician de. dares, be found that Bavaria comes second on the list, with an average of about 20 volumes to every hundred in- habitants, as against Italy, which comes next with 16, France with 12i-, Prussia with 11, and finally Russia with less than 1. As to the individual libraries, the largest in size is that of Paris, with something over two million volumes; the British Museum comes second,but a long way behind, with one million • Munich third, with 800,000 ; then Berlin, with 700,000 ; Dresden with 500,000; and Vienna, with 420,000. The library of the Vatican is not nearly so large as most people suppose. It is set down as containing only 30,000 printed books; but then it is very rich in valuable manuscripts, the total number of which is reckoned at 25,000. The most celebrated and largest of the University libraries are the Bodleian at Oxford and that of Heidelburg, each of which is set down as possessing about 300,000 volumes. CARLYLE AND ms WlFE.—Every line he has written about his wife testifies to a gratitude and an affection which are a greater glory to Carlyle than all the achievements of his genius, al* go far to atone for the unjust way in which he too often speaks of other people. There are many pages in his "Reminiscences" of simple, affectionate prattling that it is impossible to read without deep emotion:—" Ala me! she never knew fully, nor could I show her in my heavy-laden, miserable life, how much I had at all times re- garded, loved, and admired her. No telling of her now. Five minutes more of your dear company in this world.'" Here is his reminescences of the arrival at the house in Cheyne Row which be made famous for so many years:— "Her arrival .1 best of all remember: oh me! She was clear for this poor house (which she gradually, as poverty a little withdrew after long years' pushing, has made so beautiful and comfortable) in preference to all my other samples; and here we spent our two-and-thirty years of hard battle against fate; hard but not quite unvictorious, when she left me, as in her car of heaven's fire. My noble one! I say deliberately her part in the stern battle, and except myself none knows how stern, was brighter and braver than, my own. Thanks, darling, for your shining .words and,acts, which were continual in my eyes, and in no other mortal's. Worthless I was your divinity, wrapt in your perpetual love of me and pride in me, in defiance of all men and things. Oh, was it not beautiful, all this that I have lost for ever! And I was Thomas the Doubter, thel unhoping ; till now the only half-believing, in myself and my pricgless opulences ! At my return from Annandale,' after French Revolution,' she so cheerily recounted to me all the good 'items ;' item after item. ' Oh, it has had a great success, dear r —to no purpose; and at length beauti- fully lost patience with Me for my incredulous humour. Mv life has not wanted at any time what I used to call 'desperate hope' to all lengths; but of common 'hoping hope' it has had but little; and has been shrouded since youtbhood (almost since boyhood, for my school-years, at Annan, were very miserable, harsh, barren, and worse) in continual gloom and grimness, as of a man set too nakedly versus the devil and all men. Could Ibe easy to live with? She flickered round me like perpetual radiance, and in spite of my glooms and my misdoings, would at no moment cease to love me and help me. What of bounty too is in heaven!" RETROSPECTIVE GLANCE AT SEASONS AND People are are apt to say such and such a season was the worst they ever saw or heard of, but I have often heard old people talk of the bad years at the beginning of the century, and allude to a few years about 1812 and 1816—one in particu- lar, cold and wet. The corn was not ingathered until the January following. The only good day of the week was the Sunday, and a good deal of the corn was carried on that day of the week. The bread, no matter what corn it was made of, would not stay in the oven. An immense quan- tity of land was sown with wheat up to the end of the Pen- insular war until it would not grow a new corn: for an old one it cost more for seed than it returned in crop; and a deal of the poor land was never sown with grass seeds at all, but allowed to become permanent pasture as it could. Look at the difference caused by long drought and heat- -1825 was dry and hot; 1826 dry, but much greater heat. Harvest was over middle of July. Wheat was the only crop which produced any quantity of straw. Thousands of acres of barley were never out in ear; still the corn weighed 591 b: per bushel. Oats a great part pulled, they were so short; and in Scotland, where they were used for meal, they were so full of sand the meal was unfit for food. Thatch could not be found for the ricks, and rushes and sedges were cut from the river sides in lieu of straw. The root crops were scant and irregular. Cattle and sheep had to be driven miles to water. Wool was badly washed. Flax was steeped in the rivers, thereby killing the fish. In 1827 the drought broke up; 1828, 1829, 1830 were wet, bad harvests, wheat mostly sprouted. Professor Beesley repeated his belief that no new national organisation was advisable or possible, but ultimately it was resolved to form a Democratic Confedera- tion, and to summon a conference of delegates from Great Britain and Ireland. Among the principles included'in the new programme are the nationalisation of the land, the abolition of house lands, bribery at elections being declared felony, and legislative independence for Ireland. Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, M.P. says, writing to a. Hull gentleman with reference to the formation and usefulness of Jutior Liberal Associations, that such organisations help to spread among all classes an intelligent interest in politics, and, bringing together as they do the most active and earnest of the yoong.er members of the Liberal party, they have been enabled, in many cases, to do good service to the common cause. We are, the right hon. gentleman adds, in the midst of great changes, both at home and abroad, and as he believe., changes greater still are immediately before us. There never was a time when it was more im- portant that every Liberal should be able to give a reason for the faith which IC in him, and should aid, according to is opportunities, in the furtherance of the principles to which he is attached. A very serious accident has occurred on the South- Eastern line, near Folkestone. At the Abbotsclifle Tunnel an immense quantity of chalk cliff, estimated at about 20,000 tons, has slipped and blocked the line. PEACE PRESKEYATION (Irtatawn) Brtm.—The Royal assent was given by Commission to this bill. SOUTH GARSTON DOCK :11.ND RAILWAY BILL.-011 the 3rd instant, on application of the promoters of this bill, an order was passed that it should not be further proceeded with this session. EARL CADOGANt the chairman of the select committee to wtich the bill was referred, now moved that this order be discharged, and that the bill be recom- mitted to the same committee for the purpose of considering the question of awarding costs to the petitioners who ap- peared before the cOmmittee. The promoters of the bill object th its being recommitted merely to decide the question of costs. The MARQUIS Of LANSDOWNE, who supported the promoters' view of the course that should be taken, said he had a large number of petitions from merchants and others of Liverpool and neighbourhood praying that the bill might be recommitted upon its merits. Eventually the debate was adjourned in order to afford time for agreeing what course should be adopted with respeet to the bill. AFGHAN AVFAIRS.—Lord ENFIELD made a statement on Indian affairs, stating that the revised figures showed that the expenditure to the 31st May, 1881, showed these results —Military operations, £15,516,000; frontier rail ways expen- diture, £4,058,000; total, £19,574,000. The further state- ment he had to lay on the table related to Candahar. He said that immediately after the decision had been taken not permanently to occupy Candahar, communications were opened with the Ameer, informing him of the de- cision of the Government to reconsider the arrange- ments which had been made for the government of Southern Afghanistan, and expressing the desire of the Viceroy to act in the mattet in consultation and concert with him. The Ameer expressed his gratitude to the British Government, and his strong desire for a personal interview with the Viceroy to confer upon the affairs of Afghanistan, but this, on account of the Viceroy's illness, and for other reasons, WAS deemed at the time impossible. However, he bad sent an Envoy to confer on the subject. The Viceroy had since informed the Ameer that it was necessary that the Cabal troops, with a Governor authorised to receive the charge from the British officers, should reach Candahar early in Apia. The Amcor replied that he was desirous of taking possersion of Candahar at once, that his troops were all ready, and that he hoped his forces would reach Candahar about the time named. The last information was that the Cabul troops bad started, or would shortly start, from Cabul, and would reach Candahar early in April, and that all arrangements for withdrawal were complete. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.

POSTMEN'S CHEISTHIAS BOXES.—Mr. FAWCETT said that he believed the estimate that the letter carriers received in Christmas boxes as much as 5s a week for each man if spread over the whole year was far too large. He did not think it desirable to grant an addition to their pay in lieu of Christmas boxes, for he believed the public would still con- tinue to give them—(cheers)--but he was decidedly of opinion that they ought not to ha asked for with importu- nity, and he had last year issued a circular to this effect. which he believed had been generally obeyed, as there bad not been a single complaint on the part of the public. (Cheers.) CINDAHAR.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON made a state- ment respecting Candahar similar to that submitted to the House of Lords. He intimated that the correspondence and papers on the subject were at present incomplete.—ln answer to a question from Sir George Balfour, he intimated that further papers from India on the subject of military expenditure would be in the hands of members in the course of a few days. BENEFIT SOCIETIES—Lord F. CAVENDISH said he could not, without more definite information as to the proposed legislation imposing further restrictions on the registration of benefit societies and their meeting at public-houses, say whether the Government would be inclined to assist it. There had not yet been full experience of the working of the Act of 1875, and, without clear proof of its necessity, further restrictions might do more harm than good. As far as he was informed, the failure of friendly societies had not been mve constant than that of other classes of companies. With respect to public-houses, it must be remembered that in many places there was no other accommodation available, and the great number of the—he hoped the majority— were perfectly respectable. It might interest the honourable member to know that the bulk of the societies which had reached 100 years of age and upwards met at public-houses, amongst them being the oldest English society, which was founded in 1687, and the third oldest, founded 1708, and others ranging in age from 117 to 194 years. THE BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.—IMPORTANT STATEMENT. —Mr. BAXTER asked the First Lord of the Treasury on what day he proposed to make the financial statement.— Mr. GLADSTONE : lam now in a position to answer this question • and, as there is an expectation that to-day the I House will be informed as to the course of business, I may take the opPortunity to state what we, propose respecting it. I presume that we shall to-night dispose of the necesssary business in supply, as well as possibly to get rid of some of that which is not so urgent. It is generally understood that, that being so, the motion with regard to Candahar ' will come on on Thursday, and it will be very desirable in. deed, if the debate is to be prolonged into a second night, that we should arrange to take the second night's debate on Friday. That is what we should endeavour to promote. I will not say anything about the particular days of next week ,except that we have the Mutiny Bill on hand, and, should it require time for discussion, the proper time will no doubt be found next week. That carries us to the end of the month, and I should propose :to make the financial statement on Monday, the 4th of April. I should then also hope on Thursday, the 7th of April, that we may be able to introduce the Irish Land Bill. (Ministerial cheers.) on Friday, the Bth April, we should propose the adjournment of the House two or three days earlier than the usual time, involving the loss of one day, or one day and a half only at the most, but after the very long sitting of the House I think that is an arrangement which will be satisfactory to everyone. (Cheers.) Then we should propose to meet again on Monday, the 25th, which, relatively to Easter on the 17th, would be the usual date. AS we should have had thins vacation of reasonable length, and as the Irish Land Bill will have been in the hands of members and before the country for a considerable time, and as it is very desirable not to lose time in prosecuting the discussion upon it, we shoulii also propose, and I am anxious that this should be understood, that we should take the commencement of the debate on the 'second reading when the House meets on Monday. the 25th. MR. BRADLAUGH'S APPLICATION FOR THE CHILTERN HUNDNEDS.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply to a question from Earl Percy, said an application had been made to him for the Chiltern Hundreds on the part of honourable member for Northampton. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. GORST, replying to a question, said, finding that there was to be an appeal against the decision recently given against Mr. Bradlaugh, he should not in the meantime proceed with his motion for a new writ for Northampton. . .

......-- _ Mg. O'DONNELL'S SESPENSION.-011 the motion to go into Supply, Mr. O'DoNNELL brought before the House for review the circumstances under which he was suspended for a second time a fortnight ago, and moved a resolution de- claring that the Chairman was in error in informing the Rouse that Mr. O'Donnell was contravening his authority. Explaining the misunderstanding, which he said had arisen in consequence of the interruption from the other side, he assured the House that when the Chairman refused to licar him and ultimately "named" him, he was not intending, as the Chairman supposed, to revert to the point of order already decided (Mr. Finigan's use of the words "beastly bellowing"), but to call the attention of the Chair to the clamorous and discourteous interruptions of certain Radical members.—Mr. PLAYFAIR referred at length to the details of the occurrence, pointing out that they could not convey any other impression to his mind than that Mr. O'Donnell was endeavouring to raise a discussion on Mr. Finigan's language, and that it would not have been regular at that moment to have called attention to the interruptions of whitl he complained.—Mr. GLADSTONE agreed that Mr. O'Donnell had shown that he had no intention to challenge the authority of the Chair; but he could not agree in a resolution which declared the Chairman to have acted erroneously, as it was quite clear thatif he had been misled it was by Mr. O'Donnell.—Sir STAFFORD NORTRCOTE took the same view,and drew the moral that the impatience mani- fested in certain quarters of the House was very greatly responsible for the heat of these scenes.—Mr. O'DortNILL withdrew his motion. THE ARMY ESTIMATES.—In moving the Supplementary 'Vote cf £44,600 for warlike stores and supplies for the cam- paign in the Transvaal, Mr. CHILDERS intimated that it might possibly be necessary to ask for some additional amount; but that se far as the War Office was able to form an estimate the present vote would suffice.—After a short discussion, Mr. T. D. &JUJU-NT forced his protest against the vote to a division, but the vote was agreed to by 106 to 6.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESIDAY. CONCLUSION OF PEACE WITH THE BOERS. Earl Kim- berley informed the House that he had received a summary of the terms arranged between Sir-E. Wood and the Boer leaders. The noble Earl then read the summary, which had I previously been communicated to the House of Commons. ' C"lrr OF 84%1°N (SCOTLAND) BILL.—The Lord Chan- cellor moved that the House resolve itself into a committee on the Court of Session (Scotland) Bill. After some dis- cussion Lord Moncrieff moved the adjournment of the debate to afford time for further consideration of the subject. The Lord Chancellor, in consequence of the course the discussion had taken and the strong feeling that had been aroused in Scotland in regard to the Bill, assented to the motion for adjournment, and said he should probably not ask the House to proceed further with the measure this session. The debate was adjourned accordingly. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. CANDIHAR.—Sir It CARDEN presented a petition from 2,000 citizens of London in public meeting assembled that day, praying the House to address Her Majesty in favour of the retention of Candahar. (Conservative cheers and counter-cheers.) SUCCESS OF THE TRANSVAAL PEACE NEQOTIATIONS.— Mr. GLADSTONE said : The intelligence that Sir E. Wood has arrived at an arrangement with the Boers, and that the Boers have substantially accepted he proposals of Her Majesty's Government, is correct. (Ministerial cheers.) The right honourable gentleman went on to say that papers on the subject would be presented forthwith, and these would explain the course which had been taken by Sir E. Wood, and his arrangements, which of course he had re- ferred home; but in the meantime it might be convenient for him to state what were the main propositions of the Government. First, the suzerainty of the Queen over the Transvaal is acknowledged. (Cheers.) Second, complete self-government promised to the Boers. Third, the control of the foreign relations reserved. Fourth, there is to be a resident nt the future capital. Fifth, the royal commission

- o shall consist of Sir Hercules Robinson, Sir Evelyn Wood, and Chief Justice Villiers, of the Cape. Sixth, the com- mission will consider the provisions for the protection of native interests and arrangements as to frontier affairs. Seventh, the commission will also consider the question of whether any and what portions of the Transvaal territory eastwards within certain limits should be severed from the Transvaal. Eighth, the Boers withdraw from the Nek and. disperse to their homes. Ninth, the British garrisons re-, main in the Transvaal until the final settlement. Tenth{ the Boers having engaged as above, Sit E. Wood promises not to advance or send warlike stores into the TAW veal. (Cheers.) Sir S. If owertectrra : What is medal by the expression °Foreign relations reserved!' Does it mean reserved for settlement by the oom- mission, or is it taken out and reserved to the Crown?— Mr. GLADSTONE : In these words I have cited the telegram I have received, but I do not entertain the slightest doubt as to the meaning of these words. The meaning I take to b.? that the settlement of foreign affairs is entirely reserved to the Crown and the British Government.—Sir W. 'BART- TSLOT asked was it to be understood that the Boers bad not agreed to lay down their arms?—Mr. GLADSTONE: The terms demanded by her Majesty's Government was the withdrawal of the force and the dispersion of the Boers. As to delivering up their arms we have never asked any such thing. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Tomo] inquired as to the use of the word suzerainty; was it synonymous with sovereignty, or was any distinction made 11—Mr. GLADSTONE : The word suzerainty in modern times, I believe, is perfectly well known in international affairs. It is quite distinct from sovereignty undoubtedly, while it has relations to sove- reignty. But it would not be convenient for me now to give a legal distinction, nor would I attempt to go further than the general statement I have made wishing that honourable gentlemen should reserve their judgment until they have the opportunity of considering the matter when the docu- ments we shall lay before the House are in their hands.— Lord R. Cittriacniu, wished to know if it was to be under- stood from the telegram just read that relations between the British Crown and the Transvaal will be analogous to the relations between the Sultan and Eastern Rouraelia. (A laugh.)—Mr. GLADSTONE : So far analogous as that the re- lations of suzerainty will obtain in both cages; but I can- not say that the Transvaal will adopt the East Roumelian constitution.

FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE.—Mr. CHAPLIN proposed A motion to the effect that the recent outbreak of foot and mouth disease was due to the importation of animals from abroad, that the present regulations as to such importation were not a sufficient safeguard against contagion, and that until the council were satisfied that there was no disease among the cattle of any foreign country, such cattle should not be permitted to enter British ports. After a long and tedious discussion, in the course of which no new fact or argument was adduced, on a division 147 members voted for the resolution and 205 against it. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAT.

- - AGRICIIIIITIAL TENANTS' COMPENSATION BILL. Mr. CHAPLIN moved the second reading of the Agricultural Tenants' Compensation Bill, the object of which, he ex- plained, was to remedy the defects which experience had showed to exist in the operation of the Agricultural Hold- ings Act of 1875; an Act which, he said, had failed to give to the tenants in all cases the security which it was intended to provide. He proposed to effect this object by making the Act compulsory in all cases, and he would do this in three ways: First, the landlord and tenant ought to adopt the provisions of the Act of 1875 itself; secondly, they ought to adopt the schedule system, which was, in fact, the Lincolnshire custom; and, thirdly, they might adopt a special contract, according to the locality, situation, and the circumstances of the case; and in the absence of any of these courses they would come under the Act itself. This, he argued, would secure a bond fide compensation.- -Mr. HOWARD thought the bill under consideration would not prove an effective remedy for the object its promoters had in view, and, if remedial measures were to be applied, they ought, in his view, to be far more reaching and com- prehensive. This bill failed to deal with some of the graver defects of the Agricultural Holdings Act, but he should prefer it to the bill of the member for North Devon, because it appeared to him to be an honest attempt to grapple with the question, and it hit one of the greatest blots of the act of the late Government, viz., the permissive clauses.— Several hon. members, who speak with authority on agri- cultural matters, opposed the bill, on the ground that it was utterly inadequate to meet the wants of the British farmer.l What was required, these gentlemen pointed out, was a system by which full compensation could be secured to the tenant for such enhanced letting value of his holdieff' as was due to his own outlay and skill ; and Mr. Barclay argued that the only method of effecting this reform, which was essential if farmers were to have freedem and confidence in their own enterprises, was to give them perpetual leases of the soil. But although the bill was generally regarded as a sort of supplementary Christmas box to the farmers, in- tended to delude them into the belief that it gave them all they could possibly require, the Government very wisely refrained from opposing it.—Sir W. Hancomer, in an effective speech, sarcastically remarked that he sup- posed the atmosphere of Opposith n had given greater activity and energy to the farmers' friends. He congratulated Mr. Chaplin upon "the intellectual progress" which his proposals indi- cated. Sir William also remarked that, like many other "great and statesman-like" measures proceeding from the Tory party, the Act of 1875 seemed to require a great deal of amendment, more particularly in its fundamental prin- ciples. He said that the Government would not offer any opposition to the bill at the stage of second reading, but he could not agree to the suggestion that the bill should be referred to a Select Committee, for the House itself was capable of dealing with it as it stood. He hoped that before , this Parliament ended those who represented the Liberal party would undertake to deal with this question on more' intelligible principles and upon a more solid foundation.— After some characteristic remarks by Lord ELCHO, who opposed the bill on the ground that all the farmer wanted was more sunshine, the measure was read a second time.— A bill for the re-enfranchisement of Sligo was lost by 180 votes to 30.

270.—Currizra TRREH SETS OF TEETH.

The granulated walls of the gums sruounding an alveolus from which a tooth has been extracted, may become covered with mucous membrane, before the socket is filled with a deposit of new bone, or at any rate, of the surfaces of the duplicated membrane near the bone, and wherever such arrangement or condition of this tissue does take place upon the alveolar border, it is probable that the new tooth papilla is produced, which in the progress of its devolopment, is attended by the formation of the various appendages neces- sary to the production of a perfect tooth. R. M. Carow, L.D.S.

271.—HELIOSCOPE. The belioscope is a telescope, behind which the image of the sun is received upon a planed surface. An astronomical telescope is drawn out a little further than is necessary for common use, and directed towards the sun, the image of which is formed, is received in a dark place. For this pur- pose a dark chamber is employed, or the telescc,pe is placed in a dark, funnel-shaped enclosure, the bottom of which is covered with oil paper or closed with ground glass, oA which the sun's image is formed. Upon this paper or glass a circle Is described, equal to the Image, and divided, by five con- centric circles, into twelve digits. With this instrument the spots on the sun, eclipses, &c., may be observed without Injuring the eyes. For greater exactness, however, it is better to observe the sun through a telescope, the glasses of which are smoked or coloured. Astronomical telescopes are commonly provided with coloured plane glass, which may 6e screwed on when the sun is to be observed. P. W. FAIR, Warrington.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS. -THURSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS. -THURSDAY.

CANDAHAR.—Lord WAVENEY intimated that on Tuesday he should ask which Government, the Indian or Afghan, re- ceived at present the yearly revenue of Candahar' and sub- ject to what account, and in the event of Candahar being transferred to the Government of Abdur Rahman, what moans for the protection of British subjects would be adopted, and whether a consul, with right of flag and escort, would be appointed to reside in that city. Tun Tniarswear...,Lord BRABOCRNE asked what arrange- ments had been made for the protection of loyal Boers and natives and Englishmen settled in the Transvaal, and whether the " murderers " of Colonel Anstruther and his men were to be brought to justice.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY read a telegram from Sir Evelyn Wood, in which it was stated that there was to be "no molestation" on either side for political acts, and that the attack on Colonel Anstruther came under the description of "acts of civilised warfare," for which a complete amnesty had been recorded. Sir E. Wood's telegram contains a significant reference to the " hitherto inert power" of the loyalists in the Transvaal. BASIITOLAND.—Lord BELMORB called attention to the war in Basutoland, and asked whether the prerogative of peace and war rested with the Ministers at Capetowm—The Earl of KIMBERLEY (Colonial Secretary) replied that the Cape Ministers were supreme in all questions arising within their own territories. He repeated the expression of his views as to the origin of the war, and said that at the proper time he should again impress on the Cape Government the necessity and policy of granting fair and reasonable terms to the Basutos. Before the House rose it was announced that the Easter recess would, as regards the Peers, extend frurn April 7th to May 4. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY.

- - A WHISKEY WAPINSCHAW.—IO reply to Sir W. Lawson, the Lord ADVOCATE said that his attention had been called to the proposed "whiskey wapinschaw " at Elgin. He did not quite know what a whiskey wapinschaw meant—whether it was a reward for the best whiskey or for the greatest con- sumer. (Laughter.) He had directed the procurator-fiscal to inform the lord provost that if there was any lottery the parties would be liable to be prosecuted. EvicTions us IRELAND.—In reply to Mr. T. P. O'Connor and others, Mr. FousTEu said that the statements made by Mr. Sexton with respect to certain evictions by which 5,000 families would be evicted were greatly exaggerated. It was a fact that when the Coercion Bill was passed there had been a great decrease, as compared with the previous year, in the number of applications for decrees and writs of eject- ment in consequence of the non-payment of rent. THE SUGAR BOUNTIES CONFERENCE.—Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN stated, in answer to Mr. Whitley, that inquiries had been made of the Governments of France, Belgium Ger- many, Holland, and Austria as to whether they would agree to take part in an international conference on the question of the removal of bounties on the import of sugar. The Belgian and Austrian Governments had signified their willingness to take part in such a conference. The German and Dutch Governments had declined. The French Government had signified their willingness to accept a conference subject to a preliminary agreement on the part of each of the negotiating Powers to adopt common measures for suppressing premiums on the export abroad of refined sugar, such measures to include restrictions upon the im- port of sugar from countries where bounties were still allowed to continue. CANDAHAR. LORD RARTINOTON announced that the troops of the Ameer, to whom Southern Afghanistan is to be transferred, were already marching from Cabot to Canda- liar in order to take possession of the latter province, and said it was not expected that they would meet with resistance. THE TRANSVAAL—RECALL OF RHINFORCEMENTS.—Mr. GLADSTONE announced that telegrams had been despatched to Capetown apprising Sir Frederick Roberts of the close of the war and recalling him to England, with General Newdi- gate and nearly all the troops now en route to Natal. The final settlement of the whole matter is to be left in the hands of Sir E. Wood. SEDITIOUS SPEECHES IN IRELAND. In answer to Vis- count Folkestone as to the recent speech by Mr. Dillon, M.P. in which he said that Judge Fitzgerald had better take care that the Land League did not do away with him and ,his salary, Mr. FORSTER said he did not think it wise, in the public interest, to state whether the Government intended to take any steps in the matter. • THE WITHDRAWAL OF TROOPS FROM CANDAEAR —Mr. •E. STANHOPE moved: "That, in the opinion of this House, the withdrawal of British troops from Southern Afghanistan in the present critical state of affairs in that country will not be conducive to the true and permanent interests of India." The hon. gentleman marshalled his arguments against the surrender in the familiar form, and concluded by protesting against the policy of
MR. BRIGHT ON MR. HERMON'S ARGUMENTS FOR PROTECTIoN.

A Preston gentleman, who sent to the Right Hon. John Bright the speech of Mr. Hermon, M.P., delivered last week, at the demonstration in the Area of the Corn Exchange, Preston, has received the following reply from Mr. Btight 182, Piccadilly, March 18th, 1881. Dear Sir,— I have read Mr. Hermon's speech to which you refer me. lam not amazed at the ignorance it displays or its misrepresentation of facts. He does not tell how he proposes to protect by new tariff duties the factory workers or the mill workers of Preston. His constituents are ex- porters of cotton goods to all quarters of the globe; they compete with all foreign manufacturers in all foreign markets. How can he protect them by reimposing duties on the import of cotton goods, which they so largely export? Does he intend to give a bounty out of the general taxes on all goods they export, as he says "he would give a bonus on every acre of land that a farmer of this country chooses to till and crop with corn ?" He proposes to give oat of the taxes a bonus, how much he does not say, but so much per acre on all land growing corn, doubtless to enable the farmers to pay a higher rent than the land is Worth, and to limit our supplies of corn from the United States, Canada, and other countries! Mr. Hermon did not tell his audience that between the harvests of 1879 and 1880, that is in the year after the bad harvest of 1379, out of every four loaves of bread eaten by the people of the United Kingdom three loaves came from abroad, and that in no other year in his lifetime or in mine have our people been fed so cheaply or on bread of such excellent quality. What must Mr. Hermon think of the mental condition of his constituents when he ventured to utter to them the con- fused nonsense of his speech, and what must every intelli- gent elector of your town think of a representative in Par- liament who has not advanced a step beyond the benighted ignorance of forty years ago? If you wish to see this question of free trade and our trade well discussed, I advise you to pay sixpence for the little book published by Messrs. Cassell, Petter, and Galpin, of London, entitled "Free Trade and English Commerce," written by Mr. Mongredin. I wish every elector in Preston could have it and read it, and I may recommend it to Mr. liermon.as a book out of which he may begin to learn some- thing of correct facts and sound arguments on the question of free trade, and on the results of our policy as adopted by Sir Robert Peel and Mr. Gladstone since the year 1841. I have not time to write you at greater length. The little book I have mentioned will tell you the truth on the facts and results of our free-trade policy.—l am, very truly yours, JOHN Barony.

Sir CHARLES DILKE met the taunt that we were withdrawing from Afghanistan at the moment Russia was advancing in Central Asia, by announcing that the first act of Alexander 111, was to recall General Scobe- I eef to St. Petersburg and to put a stop to operations in which that general had engaged. div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: THE IRON AND COAL TRADES.

Battnow, Monday.—A steadier tone is reported in the hematite pig iron trade this morning, and more business is being transacted both by home and foreign buyers. Makers are very fully employed, and the output of both Bessemer and forge iron is considerable on all hands. Makers are well sold forward, and are likely to remain so, for orders have lately come in more plentifully, and it seems reasonable to suppose that in the course of another month or two the work now in hand will be supplemented by several spring orders on home and foreign account. Prices have not moved from last week's quotations, the figure at which business has been done ranging from 60s. to 635. at the works. Steel workers are busy, and the demand active. Iron ore and coal in brisk request.

LANCAMRE.—There is very little material change to re- port in the condition of the coal trade of this district since last week. Easiness throughout continues quiet. and sup- plies of all descriptions of fuel are plentiful in the market. For the better qualities of round coal suitable for house-fire purposes there is still a fair demand, but the lower classes of round coal for manufacturing purposes are rather a drug, the depression in the shipping trade tending to throw a good deal of common round coal upon the home market; and at some of the collieries stocks are accumulating. Engine classes of fuel move off tolerably well, but with the consider- able quantity of slack at present being produced, supplies generally are fully equal to requirements, and burgy is plentiful. So far as prices are concerned the market contin- ues weak, and although there is no very material alteration in the quoted rates, the tendency of the market is down- wards, both as regards local and outside district coals. The average prices asked by Lancashire colliery proprietors at the pit month are as under: Best coal lOs to 10s 6d per ton seconds, 7s 6d to 8s 6d ; common round coals, 5s 6d to 6s 6d, burgy 5s to 5s 6d, and slack 3s 6d to 4s 6d per ton, accord- ing to quality. There is, however, a want of firmness amongst sellers in adhering to their quotations, and tie maximum rates quoted above are only being obtained in ex- ceptional cases, concessions being made to secure orders, which, as far as round coals are concerned, aro gradually bringing prices back to their old level. The demand for coke is only limited at the prices quoted last week. Extreme depression continues throughout the iron trade of this dis- trict, and not only are very few orders being given out, but there is a complete absence of any inquiries of any im- portance, any business doing being confined almost entirely to small retail lots. The tendency of prices continues downwards. Lancashire makers of pig iron are still asking 45s 63 for forge and 46s 6d for foundry, less 21, delivered equal to Manchester, and at about these figures small sales are being made, but for anything like good orders local makers are open to offers at under the above rates. In outside brands coming into this district all kinds of figures are men- tioned as those which sellers would be willing to take, and merchants in some cases have evidently commenced "bear- ing" operations, but there are so few actual transactions that it is scarcely possible to soy what prices really are. Some of the local finished-iren works continue tolerably well employed completing old orders, but there is very little new work coming in, and prices are weak. For delivery into the Manchester district the average figure at winch ordinary bars can be bought 19 about £5 17s 6d; hoops, £6 10s to £7; common plates, £7 lOs ; and sheets, £7 12s 6d to £7 15s per ton. Founders generally are short of work, and to secure orders very low prices are being quoted.

1881. LUNACT IN LANCASHIRE.
_ - _ AN INTERESTING REPORT.

On Saturday, the reports of the visitors and superinten- dents of the various county lunatic asylums for the past year were issued to the justices from the office of the Clerk of the Peace. Xhe following refers to Rainhill Asylum:— It is reported by the Committee of Visitors of this asylum that the institution has been full, and that many patients had been sent to other asylums at a considerable distance. The plans and specifications for the proposed new buildings are approaching completion. The alterations and additions to the old building are proceeding, and will supply a long- acknowledged want, as the asylum is now receiving nearly double the number of patients provided for in its original i construction. Mr. T. L. Rogers, the medical superintendent, states in his report that thoonumber of patients admitted in the past year was 196, including 14 re-admissions; that for 1879 be- ing 171, including 16 re-admissions. The average number under treatment during the year WAS 684' in 1879 it was 6E5. The reduction was caused by a few beds being thrown out of use. The admissions included 18 cases of general paralysis, and 20 of epilepsy. One man and one woman were admitted in a moribund state, and survived only two days after admission. In three cases there was no evidence I of insanity. Eighty-five patients were discharged asl recovered, including the three just mentioned, and of these five were re-admitted within a short period. In the case of one patient discharged from this asylum about Easter, Mr. Rogers says it has come to his knowledge that the man hay since been an inmate of two other asylums, and will there- fore figure as two admissions and three recoveries in one year. It is an open question whether euch patients can ever be properly called "recovered." Sixty patients have been discharged as relieved, or improved, chiefly to the workhouses including six who escaped. Fifty-nine patients have died, the causes of death being chiefly of a chronic nature. The deaths include four patients who had been in- mates from 24 to 29 years. One of these had been employed during the whole period of 29 years as clerk and steward. Although the subject of a fixed delusion, and of hallucina- tions of hearing, he was thoroughly trustworthy and accu- rate in his accounts, having apparently the faculty of being able to separate in his work his insane individuality from the sane; and although permitted certain advantages and indulgences over other patients, he never in any way took an undue advantage of them, or abused the trust that was reposed in him, both these conditions, the moral and the in- tellectual, being in Mr. Roger's experience unique in the history of an insane patient. He died at 73 years of age. As to the table of causes of insanity, which has for the last three years been sent to the Commiksioners in Lunacy, there appears to be some difference of opinion as to its usefulness, seeing how very difficult it is in the majority of cases to assign any one definite cause for a state which involves a change of the nervous constitution of the entire individual. With the exception ef certain physical causes, such as in- temperance in the form of bouts of excessive drinking. direct injury to the bead, and of some moral causes, such as shocks of sudden fright, severe domestic affliction, or sudden reverses of fortune, it is always difficult, and not infre- quently erroneous, to ascribe so great a change from health to disease as is comprised in the term insanity to any one definite proximate cause. By far the most prolific of any one cause must be reckoned alcoholic intemperance. It accounts for 30 per cent, of insanity in the men, and for more than 10 per cent, in the women, treated at this asylum. Mr. Rogers says the theory has been advanced by some medical writers that 4runkenness if often an effect of in- sanity rather than a cause; but he believes that those who advance that view have not carried their inquiries below the surface.

div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Wed- nesday afternoon, Councillor Cook"presiding. There were also present Councillors Bishop,' and Owen, Mr. Craik (deputy town clerk), and Messrs. Bamford, aud Dutton (school attendance officers.) Mr. CRAIK having read the minutes of the last meeting they were "signed as correct."

THE GUARDIANS AND SCHOOL FEES. Mr. CRAIIC read a circular letter from Mr. Herbert Belly, chairman of a conference of ,public bodies held in Manchester, on the llth inst., to consider, the question of the payment of school fees in cases of poverty. The bodies represented were the Liverpool, Bootle, and Manchester School Boards, the Louth (Lincolnshire) School Attendance Committoe, and the Guardians of the poor for Manchester, Chorlton, and Bolton. The conference resolved that it was desirable that section 10 of the Elementary Education Act, 1876, should be amended, so ass to transfer from the Poor Law Guardians to the Local Authorities, under :that Act the statutory duty of paying the school fees of children, whose parents not being paupers, are unable by reason of poverty to pay such fees. After the Liverpool representatives had left the meeting, the following resolution was adopted, "That the duty of appointing School Attendance Committees be removed from Boards of Guar- dians." The representatives from Bolton, and Louth did not vote upon the second resolution, stating that they were not aware that such a subject would be proposed, and that they had not been authorised to vote upon it. It was resolved also to forward copies of the resolution to the School Board, School Attendance Committees, and Boards of Guardians of Lancashiee ar.d Cheshire, and to ask for their co-operation. Mr. Beiley therefore asked for an early reply to the effect that the St. Helens council were authorised to offer that co- operation. Mr. CHAIR said if the committee agreed to the proposal the money would have to come out of the borough funds. The committee declined to agree with the proposal. OFFICERS' REPORTS.

Mr. BAMFORD reported that the four boys the committee authorised him at the last meeting to get committed to in- dustrial schools had been summoned before the magistrates and committed to the following schools:—Enunanuel Spash, to the Liverpool Certified Industrial School, Everton-terrace; William Potter, to the Liverpool School Board industrial school, Hightown; and Patrick Shea and Thomas Fitz- patrick, to the Boys' Refuge, St. Anne-street, Liverpool. Richard Delmage was discharged on license from the Liver- pool School Board industrial school on the sth of March, but had only been able to attend school twice since in con- sequence of having a sore foot from broken chilblains. During the month 1,032 absent and irregular scholars had been reported by the teachers is No.l district; the parents of 94 of the most irregular of the above children had been noticed to appear before the Investigation Committee. Ten not being able to give reasonable excuses for such irregu- larity were ordered to be summoned, and six parents having failed to appear before the committee after being noticed to , do so, were orderedto be summoned before the magistrates, with the following results:—Fif teen were fined 6d. and costs, and one boy, William Whitby, was committed to the Liverpool Certifiectlndnstrial School, for whom he should be glad to receive farther orders. One boy, David Rankin, was recommended by the Investigation Committee to be sent to an industrial schoool, and he now awaited further orders. During the month he had found truants playing in his district, and many children on the streets. A great many parents were doing everything they could to evade the Edu- cation Act, and summoning appeared to have no effect upon them. Parents were summoned on Monday last, one being fined seven times and one six times, two five times, five three times, and two twice. . . . .

Mr'. Thomas DurroN said that during the past month the names of 829 absent and irregular scholars had been sent In by the teachers of the schools in his district, and the parents were being visited and warned by him in conse- quence of such absence and irregularity. Forty-eight parents representing 91 of the most irregular of them had been brought berore the Investigation Committee, and 16 summonses were theh ordered to be taken out against parents not being able to give a reasonable excuse for their children's absence or irregularity. Fifteen had since been fined ss. each, and one school attendance order granted. In the three cases submitted to them at their last meeting as suitable cases for industrial schools, proceedings had not been instituted in one case, as the boy had attended much better since. In the other two cases the parents had been summoned, and one boy committed to the Boys' Refuge under the Industrial Schools Act, the other case being ad- journed for a month. The boy Whitley was recommended to be sent to the Liverpool Certified Industrial School, an the boy Rankin was recommended to be sent to the Boys' Refuge if the magistrates would grant a commitment.

It is reported from Eyam, Derbyshire, that the subsidence of ground over a worked-out lead mine continues. At the first slip there has been a further fall, and part of the dwelling-house has disappeared. There are three additional subsidences on a piece of green caljed the Cross. A chasm five or six yards in circumference has opened, and rumbling sounds beneath give promise of further falls. At Cressey Top, about a rood of land has disappeared, and at Bretton Hill a number of trees have disappeared in a similar chasm. A conference of the friends of religious equality w'as held at Marylebone, London, on Tuesday. The Hon. Lyulph Stanley, M.P., presided. On the motion of Mr. Carvell resolution was adopted congratulating the friends Williams,Of religioas equality on the continuous growth of public opinion in favour of disestablishment, as the effectual remedy for the evils from which the Church of England was now suffering. Other resolutions were passed setting forth that the time had arrived when the policy of disestablishment which had been adopted in Ireland, should also be applied to Scotland. Alfred W. Johnson was charged, on his own confession, at Leamington, with having murdered Lieutenant Roper, at Chatham, on the 11th Febraary. About midnight the prisoner accosted Police-constable Timm, and gave himself into custody for murdering Lieutenant Roper. He said he met him on the staircase near his quarters, and shot him with a brother officer's pistol. He could not keep the secret longer, and did not commit the murder for robbery. He stopped in Chatham six or seven days, and then left. At the police station the prisoner made a precisely similar statement, which was taken down, and he signed it. The prisoner now denied that his name was Johnson, and refused to give his name or address. He was remanded.

A letter was read dated 19th March, 1881, frOm Mr. A. Johnstone, superintendent of police, saying that he had arranged to supply policemen to deliver and collect voting papers for the election on the Bth and 9th proximo. He I should be glad to know a few days before how many policemen would be required. The cost would be 7s. 3d. per man per day.

RESIGNATION OF MR. TAYLOR. A letter was read dated Four Lane Ends, Sutton, 19th March, 1881, desiring to inform the clerk that it was his intention to resign the office as one of the guardians of the township of Sutton on the 25th inst., and he would feel obliged if the clerk would take the usual course in electing some person to fill the vacancy.; THE NEWLY APPOINTED RELIEVING OFFICER. I The following letter was read from Mr. C. M. Stuart, the newly appointed relieving officer :—"St. Helens, 17th March, 1881.—Dear Sir,—Owing to the excessive and vexa- tious delay on the part of the company to whom I have ap- plied for my bond, I have determined to apply elsewhere forthwith. Will you be kind enough to countersign the enclosed so as to enable me to expedite matters, as I am anxious to be relieved from the slights put upon me owing to the absence of the bond in question from which ' others have been exempt." Referred to the Finance Committee. THE PROPOSED NEW CHAPEL. A letter from the Local Government Board, dated 19th March:acknowledring the receipt of the Guardians' letter of the 10th inst., together with plans for the chapel proposed to be erected by the Guardians of the Frescot Union at the Workhouse; and informing the Guardians that the Board would cause the plans to be examined as soon as the state of the business in the office might permit. MAKING A POST MORTEM EXAMINATION WITIIOI7T PERMISSION.

Mary Farrell, an inmate, complained that a post mortpn o o re teed examinationk d e s ca had s. made Afterup °dneahtherthcehrieldwwerheictwh har black marks on the child; and this probably had resulted from falling off the bed. at the Kir The CLERK said that no one could make an ex tmination without the consent of the nearest relative; and he asked if he should write to the select vestry, at Liverpool, asking for an explanation. This was agreed to. THE SMALL-PDX. A letter was read from the Local Government Board stat- ing that small-pox was prevalent in South Lancashire, and asking the Board to see that a good and sufficient quantity of lymph be supplied to the medical gentlemen appointed to vaccinate. The CLERK said he had communicated with the medical gentlem en with whom the Board had contracts, and he had also given instructions to the vaccination officers to see to the prosecution of parents who were in default with the vaccination laws. COLLECTING TEE BOLED'S MONEY. Mr. SEDDON, the collector to the Board, had made out a list of moneys received during the last fortnight according to instruction& Mr. FIDLER complained that so very little money was col- lect* the collector having obtained no more than about £3O during the last fortnight. Mr. Birtcw said that some of the money was owing before Mr. Seddon became collector, and many of the debtors were gone while others were the very worst of people to deal with.

TRE WAY TO TREAT ANONYMOUS LETTERS. The CLERK said he had received an anonymous letter having reference to relief, and mentioning a poor woman in Parr. The terms of the letter were found to be at variance with the facts of the case. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS suggested the letter be put into the waste paper basket, and all others like it.

In the Westport union all the Land League candidates were elected as poor-law guardians by large majorities. At the Cork assizes, three men were charged with " Boy cottingr .7.1 r. James Hegarty. Two, Murphy and Kelleher, were convicted; the third, Callaghan, was acquitted. A Ballina telegram states that a violent threatening letter has been received by Mr. George Orme, J.P., Rahins House, Mayo. Mr. James Joint, land agent, has also received a letter warning him of an early visit from "Rory."

div.head: PRESCOT LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: PRESCOT LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

A very interesting meeting, in connection with this Asso- ciation, was held on Wednesday evening, at the King's Arms , Hotel, at which there was a very good attendance. The I chair was occupied by Mr. A. Eccles. and amongst those present were :—Messrs. W. Ty-rer, G. W. Rawlins, J. Brown, H. Rawlins, R. Doke, G. C. Buchour, W. Pownall, J. Howard, W. Beesley, W. Mackenzie, in. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the .meeting, referred to the satisfactory termination of the Transvaal peace negotiations and said he felt certain that the important communication which Mr. Gladstone made to the House of COIDIDODO OD , the previous night was most welcome to all Englishmen— ' Liberals and Conservatives equally—because it brought to a close the most disastrous episode in our history. He thought that no settlement of the business would have been • satisfactory if they had retained possession of strongholds like Candahar, as it would have been a standing menace to the people of Afghanistan. He thought the Government had shown very great wisdom, notwithstanding the opposition of the Conservative party to the withdrawal of the garrison,.in doing what they did, and he hoped it woad be a very long- I , time before our troops ever set foot in Candabar again. l Mr. H. C. Rawlins then read an ably written, interesting, I and instructive paper on " Candahar." Mr. Rawlins re- lated at considerable length the history of our former wars with Afghanistan, and said that the present war bore a 1 strong resemblance to the previous wars. The first war had I been condemned as a standing blot upon our history, and he would like to know what the Judgement of posterity would be upon the past war. He next enumerated the causes that led to our last war with Afghanistan, giving an outline of [ the negotiations that took place before the war commenced, 1 and criticised the action taken by the principal parties in the I matter. With regard to the question whether we ought to annex or restore Candahar, he adduced several strong reasons in support of the latter course. Re showed that instead of being a barrier to the so-called designs of Russia upon Afghanistan and India, it would rather assist them, as if we retained 'possession of Candahar, the Afghans would look upon the Russians as deliverers, and would join them as allies against this country. On the other hand, if the Russians were to invade Afghanistan we could more easily seize Candahar then than retain it now, and in all probability the Afghans would be inclined to co-operate with us as allies. On the motion of Mr. G. W. Rawlins, seconded ty Mr. W. Tyrer, and supported by Mr. H. C. Rawlins, the following resolution was heartily agreed to :—" That this meeting desires to record its gratification at the announcement that ; Candahar has been restored to the Ameer of Afghanistan, and expresses its hearty confidence in the general policy of the Government."—The proceedings were brought to a close _ with the usual complimentary vote of thanks to the chairman.

THE WEATHER. Boisterous and wintry weather seems to have been general', throughout the United Kingdom on Monday. So heavy has'' been the fall of snow in Scotland that another block on the[ railways was apprehended. In the neighbourhood of Mae- cheater the wind was high, Ntith intermittent showers of hail and snow, and on Monday night there was a keen frost. gl

• a A strange hitch has occurred in the proceedings for the/ election of a minister to the parish of Coupar Angus. /0 week ago it.,was discovered that in making up a list of thew' congregation entitled to vote in the election 24 names weer, omitted through two of the pages of the communion rollr sticking together. The matter was brougbt before the. Presbytery of Meigle on Monday, when the Kirk-Session of ' Coupar Angus were instructed to go back "to the point - where the error in making up the roll took place, to revise and readjust the roll," and begin work of tho election over again.

An address has been issued by the Manchester National Society for Women's Suffrage to the women electors ef the Isle of Man congratulating them on the proud position they occupy as being the first women within Her Majesty's dominions whose rights as Parliamentary electors have been recognised and legally secured. The manner in which they- make use of their newly-acquired rights will, the address 1 states, be of material significance, not only in regard to tha.. further extension of the principal of women's suffrage hen the Isle of Man, but also in the forthcoming struggle for thea44 recognition of the claims of women tos Patliamentary repre:-; notation in this country. At a meeting of the Hundred and Fifty, the General Coin/ mittee of the Coventry Liberal Association, adopted a votol of thanks with enthusiasm to Sir U. Kay-Shuttlewortb 'fs the gallant, able, and conscientious way in which be foughtat the battle of Liberalism and of purity at the late electiowat and hoping that he may shortly fine.l a place in Parliament's for which he is so 'well fitted by his high talent and personal-11_, character." The resolution was ordered to be formallyt; drawn up by the chairman and secretary of the Asaociation;.- , illuminated in the highest style of art, and forwarded to Sir Ughtred. The report of the Chester Election Commissioners has. been issued. They say that the soma expended on the election of 1880, so far as they could ascertain, was £5.000, by the Liberals and £3,900 by the Consetvatives. With respect to corrupt practices, the report observes that Mr. William Brown was one of the principal sources of corrup- tion, and rightly described himself as the much COW Of the- Liberal party. On the Conservative side it was usually the chairmen of districts who spent money corruptly. The great weapon of parliamentary warfare at Chester, however, was beer, and the party securing the public-houses secured the majority of votes. On both sides the returns of persons employed were thoroughly fraudulent. They regard party organisations for dealing wide election funds as unqualified evils. After fully considering the whole evidence, the Com- missioners find that corrupt practices extensively prevailed in 1880, and did prevail in 1874. Long lists are annexed of bribers and bribees.

For the rest, they accept the suzerainty of the Queen of England ; they accept a British resident at their cspital ; and they consent to leave the control of their external relations to the British Government, and the protection of the aboriginees in the Trans- vaal as well as the definition of their frontier at dis- puted points to the arbitrament of a British Corn. mission. Ought not these several matters as to which the Boers have agreed to subject themselves to British authority to satisfy public opinion, so far as it is reasonably satiable, in this country? We think so.

A Bum, having for its object the dosing of public houses during the hours of polling at Parliamentary elections, to be brought in by Messrs. Hussey Vivian, Hugh Mason, Carbutt, and Caine, has just been printed by order of the House of Commons. This is a proposal which cannpt fail to commend itself to all who wish to see elections fought on purely political' grounds. The labour involved in going to and from a polling station and making a very simple mark upon a balloting paper when there is not surely so ex- haustive an undertaking as to require frequent restoratives, even if the needful stimulant is to be found in gin palaces and bar parlours. We are of opinion that his neighbours would think very little of a man who pleaded that he could not possibly per- form his political duty without the aid of Scotch or Irish liquors, or that he found it impossible to make his mark without being copiously supplied with tho beverages which are stated to be made from malt and hops. The Bill tr, which we have referred pro- vides for the extension of Acts prohibiting the sale of intoxicating liquors during the whole of the polling day at Parliamentary elections both in counties and boroughs, and makes the offence of selling at such times and places punishable by monetary penal- ties. The third clause provides that nothing in the Act shall be construed to apply to the sale of liquors to lodgers, or in packet boats, or canteens: "Nor shall preclude the sale at any time at any railway station of intoxicating liquors on arrival or departure of trains, nor shall preclude the sale and consumption of food and non-intoxicating liquors in or upon any premises wherein intoxicating liquors are usually sold." We are entirely at a loss to define the reason, but for some cause or other the promoters of the Bill have thought fit to exclude from its provisions the electors of "the city of London or liberties thereof, or any parish or place for the time being subject to the jurisdiction of the Metropolitan Board of Works, or within the area contained within a circle the radius of which is four miles from Charing Cross." Is it possible that. the electors resident within this circle alone are immaculate out of all the electors in the United Kingdom, or is the beer interest so power- ful in the City of London that the promoters feel that they dare not include that district Of course it is quite possible that there may be reasons for this ex- clusion, but surely they would also apply equally to other large cities in the kingdom. We certainly should have preferred that the Bill was made ap- plicable without exception to the whole country because we are afraid that the disaffected will be apt to cavil at the idea of the London voter being pro- vided with the means to indulge in an ad libitum supply of intoxicating liquors, whilst they are sent empty away. There is not the slightest doubt that it suggests the comparison that "What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander," and that the policy of making "fish of one and flesh of another" cannot be a wholesome one, viewed in a national light.
