I hear that a very laughable spectacle—except to the hapless parties who figured prominently in it—occurred the other Sunday morning at a certain church. Some time be- fore the commencement of the morning service, a youthful couple, who aspired to be admitted into the holy state of matrimonial felicity, presented themselves before the altar. The sun shone brightly upon the would-be-bride and bride- groom and everything appeared to be auspicious; the ring was ready and there was no necessity of repeating the feat lately performed at another church in a distant locality of turning the bridegroom upside down in order to extract the marriage fees that had somehow slipped down the lining of his clothing. But here again the old adage that true love never does run smoothly was verified. The clergyman, on turning to his books, ascertained that the banns/ had only been published twice, the result being that the marriage ceremony had to be postponed for another .week and the bridal party returned disconsolately home. The residents of a respectable part of the town have had a nice bit of scandal to discuss during the last few days. It seems that a certain gentleman, who is old enough to know better, made some overtures to a sweet young damsel and arranged to meet her on a certain evening in a lonely spot frequented by lovers. The young lady who was far more artful than her admirer dreamed of, pretended to approve of all his plans, and at the appointed time duly repaired to the trysting place—but not alone! She was accompanied by a numerous array of female friends, who were all well pro- vided with eggs and flour. The sequel can be easily imagined, for no sooner did the amorous suitor appear upon the scene than he was assailed right and left with khese mis- siles. Driven to despair at the perfidy of the fair one he ran away down the road as fast as his legs could carry him followed by the whole party of indignant young ladiei, who kept up a brisk fire as long as they managed to keep the gentleman within their reach. I must confess that I regard the doings of the Salvation Army, like the action of the heathen Chinee, rather pecu- liar. The description which I have just rsceived of one of their services is decidedly impressive if it is nothing else, My informant states that after a good deal of "shouting," those "who desired salvation," were requested to come forward to the front and kneel at the " mourners' bench "while the hymn "Whiter than snow" was sung in stentorian tones. The lady " captain" then sailed majestically forward to the aforesaid" mourners' bench," and having remarked that there was about to be made "a determined onslaught on the devil's kingdom," she immediately commenced the " onslaught " by stripping with the aid of a pair of scissors all the feathers and flowers from the hats and bonnets of i every young woman who was kneeling n front of her. In this way from 20 to 30 feathers and about half as many flowers were destroyed, not oris of the fair "sinners or rather " penitent recruits" offering the slightest resistance, which many of my readers may regard as singular, when they take into consideration the innate love of the fair sex for the head gear decorations. lam al oinformed that not satisfied with having demolished "the feather and flower Outposts of Satan's kingdom," the lady captain made a further onslaught on a pair of earrings, which were taken out of a fair damsel's ears and deliberately trampled under- foot. No doubt this sort of thing may satisfy the religious cravings of an eccentric body of monen!aniacs, but I ques- tion if other people will see the necessity for such wilful destruction.

Residents in the country who visit Lowden seldom miss the opportunity, if it is afforded them, hearing a n visitingeratoritchael Houses of Parliament, on the chance of display by some of England's foremost debaters. If any of my readers should feel disposed to do this, I would whisper to them a word of advice, which they will take heed to if they value their liberty. On entering the sacred precincts of the Rouse of Commons, they must be careful not to take with them anything like a parcel—even of sandwiches—or of carrying upon their persons a petition if it is "done UP" in the shape of a package, else they may fall into the snare of the fowler. By a new order of the Sergeant-at-arms, all visitors who carry bags or parcels have to submit to the rigorous inspection of the police on duty at the Heine, and nothing henceforth will be sacred from the piercing official eye. As travellers sometimes tarry with them personalities not generally intended for public scrutiny, unpleasant revela- tions may follow if eager visitors to the House have not re- ceived timely warning of what they may expect. This regulation jam continuation of the arrangements for securing the security of Parliament. 'The powers that be" are de- termined that Guy Fawkes No. 2 shall not reach the initiatory stages necessary for "blowing old England up alive" without interruption or detection. The most ardent advocates for abolishing the House of Lords would shudder tt the thought of the end they have in view being accom- pi ished by anything so potent 103 gunpowder. • PLACCUS.

THEI LIVERPOOL AND WARRINGTON MILITARY COR" lIAND.—The Volunteers of the 13th and 14th Sub-Districts (Liverpool and Warrington) Brigade Depots will learn with regret that Colonel De Montmorency is about to vacate his Present command to take over the 68th Brigade Depot at Galway, Ireland, on the. Ist of April next, in succession to Colonel Bagot, whose term of five years has expired. , Colonel De Montmorency has only held his present con-. mand since October, 1879, having succeeded Colonel Is Berry. Colonel H. De Renzev Pigott, latent command of tl e 70th Regiment, is to be ColOnelDuMontmorency'ssuccessor Colonel Pigott served with the 83rd Regiment during the. Indian Mutiny of 1857-58, for which he holds the medal aLd clasp. He also served in New Zealand.

HALTON MUTUAL IMPEOTEMENT SOCIET2.—On Mon" day evening, Mr. G. Pennington read a paper on "Jacob." Mr' A. E. Davies occupied the chair. A capital discussion fol- lowed, in which the following gentlemen took part:— Messrs. G. Leathwood, T. Miller, R. Hughes, S. Barrow, J. Basnett, Haddock, and B. Haddock. The attendance was but fair, the weather being of a very unfavourable character. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A WESTON MAN.—On Tuesday, Thomas Woodward, aged 60, a labourer, fell from a stage, a distance of 40 feet, whilst working at the Weston Chemical Works, and was very seriously injured. He was taken to his lodgings, and attended by Dr. Robinson up to the time of his death, which took place on Thursday morning. JOHN WESLEY AS A CHERCEMAN.—A paper was read on John Wesley, on Monday evening by Mr. Pollitt, in connec- tion with the Runcorn Trinity T.Y.M.C.A. It was shOwn that Wesley was a great lover of the church, of which he said "I live and die a member," and strongly opposed the idea of separating from it, declaring that, after close ' examinations of other religious systems, be found the church nearest the scripture model. Of the functions of the clergy he had due respect, for he told his own ministers that their duty was to go forth as preachers, but not to intrude upon the legitimate work of the clergy only, the administration of sacraments. When accused of having left the church, he said it was only so far as that when they would not let him preach inside, he went outside to do so. In doctrine, Wesley held that of the church. It was the apathy of the church of those days that aroused Wesley, who did immense good; but, were he alive to-day, not only would he be a staunch member of the church, but, doubtless, would be thought by many to be a high churchman. A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Pollitt for his able and impartial paper.—Com.

DROWNING CARE AT WESTON.—SOIIIO two months ago a carter named William Talbot, 35 years of age, mysteri- ously disappeared, and although every inquiry was made and the canal dragged, no tidings could be learnt of the man, He was last seen at Sutton, on January 18th, at a quarter- past five, by a man named James Turner, who he had been assisting to load a flat. He left with a horse to go to Weston Point along the towing path of the canal, and next morning his horse was found drowned about 200 yards from the place where he started on his journey. There was a very deep snow drift at the place where the horse was found. On the 21st instant the body of the man was found in the River Weaver canal, 1 near Riley's bone works, Sutton, by John Davis, a flatman, and who got the body out. An in- quest was held at Sutton on Thursday, before Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner.—Joseph Talbot identified the body of the deceased as that of his brother, whom he had not seen since the beginning of January last.—James Turner deposed to seeing the deceased start on his journey when he was lost. 1 He was not quite sober.—John Speed, constable stationed at Sutton, said the pockets of the deceased contained 7s. 7id. in money, several keys, a pocket knife and a pocket hand- kerchief. Deceased was properly dressed with the exception of his hat. There were no marks of violence on the body.— The jury returned a verdict of "Found dead." PRIMITIVE METHODIST HOME AND FOREIGN MISSIONS.— RuNcoRN HRANCIL—On Sunday, two sermons were preached in the Greenway-road chapel, Runcorn, on behalf of the missions of this branch, by the Rev. D. Schofield, of Frod- sham. The annual missionary meeting took place in the same place of worship, on Monday evening, under the presi- dency of Mr. Thomas Norman. There were also present on the platform, the Revs. D. Schofield, W. Thornley, of War- rington; J. Morton (resident minister), Mr. Spender, and Mr Stringfellow. The Chairman, briefly referred to the im- portance of the work they were engaged in. He next spoke of the surprising amount of work of a missionary character which could be done by the help of the children. He was sure the work was God's, or otherwise it would have been crushed out long ago. There was something for everyone to do in the cause. If they could not go abroad as bearers of the glad tidings, they might at least contribute their mite to the little ones, and so encourage them in their labours.—The Rev. D. Schofield read the report, which, taken as a whole, was considered a satisfactory one. The total amount raised by their Greenway-road congregation during the year was £lO 4s Bd.—Mr. Morton said that when they looked back upon the past history of the Gospel, they had every reason to be encouraged, for in many countries it had proved itself to be the power of the Most High, and had done what education had failed to accomplish. There were no victories so glorious as. those which stood associated with missionary history. English men were in the habit'of eulogising the customs and manners of their own land; but it must not be forgotten that there had been a time when even England was under the degrading thraldom of Heathenism, and superstition and ignorance prevailed to an alarming extent. Through the efforts of the missionaries in Britain, the dark shadow of superstition was swept away. A great work still remained to be done in this country; for the devil owned a vast amount of territory. A certain writer had estimated that the number of people who had never yet heard of Christ would present an army of 100 miles in length and one mile in breadth. When they, in imagination, contemplated such a vast number passing into eternity without hope, he thought they would agree with him that the harvest truly was plenteous, but the labourers were few.—The Rev. W. Thornley said some persons were very much opposed to the foreign missionary work, urging that there was quite enough to do in looking after the heathens at home. This theory appeared to him to be a very selfish one. It was the duty of a people so favoured by God as Englishmen, to do some- thing in the great work of carrying to other lands the glad tidings and goodwill to men. Whilst it was true a great deal of good had been accomplished, it was still a deplorable fact tbat there were thousands, who, if they were not fol- lowed by the missiOnaries, would be left without the Gospel altogether. Nearly the whole of the vast Continent of Africa was in a state of heathenism. He believed that the time would eventually come when the dark places of the earth would be illuminated by the rays of the sun of righteousness. The usual votes of thanks having been car- ried, the proceedings terminated. WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETLNG AT RUNCORN.— On Monday the quarterly meeting, in connection with the Runcorn Wesleyan Methodist denomination, was held, pre- ceded by the usual tea, at which there was a numerous at- tendance. The Rev. J. Nowell, superintendent, presided at the meeting, which was attended by about forty friends. He reported an increase in the circuit of 14 members, with 47 on trial. It was stated that the increase was not equal to the expenditure, but this is probably owing to the circuit having undertaken to provide for another married man. The expenditure this year will be about £lOO more than it was daring the last 12 months, and this quarter a deficiency of about £2O will have to be met. The Band of Hope and tem- perance schedules were read, and showed a considerable in- crease of members on the year. The report as to the day and Sunday schools was very satisfactory, there being an increase of upwards of 100 during the 12 months. This being the meeting at which the usual invitations are given, Mr. Nowell and Mr. Bateman were unanimously invited to remain a third year in the circuit, and consented. We understand that the Rev. George Hack, of Sherborne, Dor- setshire, has been invited to be the successor of the Rev. Henry Valentine, at the Conference, and has consented.— Corn.

BRITISH AID FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY : WIDNES BRANCH. —The annual meeting in connection with the above society was held on Tuesday evening, in the schoolroom, Lacey- street, Widnes. The Rev. J. Wright—Williams, vicar of Widnes, occupied the chair, and there also present on the platform the Revs. Jelinger E. Symons, and C. Bingant (superintendent). The Chairman said that the subject be- fore them called forth Christian sympathy from every regi- ment under the banner of Christ, for, notwithstanding the different denominations they represented, they all worked for the same Master. Churchmen and Dissenters met in this work on one common platform. Whatever fault existed in the mode of warefare, it was not the Sword of the Spirit that was at fault. The weapon used in this war was the Word of God, and they were met to try to find out a method of using it with greater power. He thought it was to their own interest to help forward the cause, for in doing good they were themselves blessed.—The Rev. C. Bingant read the report which showed that the total amount sent to the parent society by the Widnes branch during the year was £l2. The Rev. J. E. Symons said that at the present time there were 200,000,000 of Bibles in the world, and for every two of these they owed one to the efforts of the British and Foreign Bible Society, by whom the book was circulated in about 238 languages. In the Scripture, eternal life vtas often typified as a river; it flowed over the thirsty country, giviag life and joy wherever it went. Therefore every new language the scriptures were translated into was cutting a new channel for this mighty river. The work of the society was divided. It was a British and Foreign Bible Society. In the British and Channel Isles, there were no fewer than six different languages spoken and the Bible Society was the only association which had sent Bibles to these different places. A great deal was being done through the medium of the colporteur. The society also tried to introduce Bibles and other books into large establishments, and hence they were to be found in almost all waiting rooms and hotels. Looking at the progress of the work in India, a wonderful spectacle presented itself. Men of experience had told them that it would be no use trying to introduce the doctrines of the book among the llindoos, as the principal thing taught in the Sriptures was faith, and the Hindoos were accustomed to work every problem out by reasoning until the result became apparent. In spite of this, the society began its work in India, and with very little result at first, for the Brahmins and Buda- hists would have nothing to do with them, bat looked down upon them with contempt. Now, in Calcutta and Allabal- had, the forms of caste were breaking down, and Christianity was winning its way. In Madras 60,000 had renounced Mahomet and the false gods of heathendom, and accepted Christ as their only Saviour. Coming a little nearer home, he said that in the city of Paris a great deal of good was being done. Not a word was spoken against the Roman Catholic religion; they simply preached Jesus Christ the corner stone. Various rooms were opened, in which they held their service, at the close of which they distributed small copies of the Bible, supplied by the Bible Society. Though, however, so much had been done in Paris, a vast Amount of ignorance of the Scriptures still prevailed there. I:ruly the fields were white unto harvest. Men were saying , • Come over and help us." It was the boast sf every Eng- ii!hman that the sun never set upon English territory. He wished them to make it their boast that the sun should never set upon the countries that had been blessed by the word of God, sent to them by English Christians A coi- -1 lection was then made, and the usual votes of thanks having been passed, the proceedings terminated.

Pram= IMPROVEMENT CLass.—The adjourned de- bate on Mr. Hobson's paper, "Sabbath observance," was resumed on Thursday evening, when a very interesting debate was taken part in by the following members: Messrs. A. White, W. H. Hughes, F. Hughes, J. W. Holding, J. Manley, R. Greenhalgh, and the chairman (Mr. W. Pickton). The debate was again adjourned. RuNcom RETELL SANITARY AtrraMarrY.—Tke fort- nightly meeting of this Authority was held. at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present—ROY. Canon Barclay (in the chair), Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. H. Neild, J. Chal- loner, W. Pickering, J. Mclntyre T. Andrews, .1. Campkin, J. Smith, sen., W. Wilkinson, J. Darbvshire, J. Weir, H. Lowe, Wm. Jackson, and H. Linaker (clerk). There was no business of public interest. .

LANCASHIRD AND CHNSIIIRD VoLuNTEnns.—The maxi mum establishment of Rifle Volunteerg in Lancashire is 20,100, the total number enrolled being 18,416, of whom 17,923 are efficients. With the exception of one or two coun- ties immedtately adjacent to the metropolis, Lancashire figures in the return just issued as a most creditable instance of the popularity of the volunteer service. The County Palantine has, so far as artillery is concerned, a maximum establishment of 6,300, and of the 6,103 enrolled, 5,768 are efficient. The Cheshire volunteers have an enrolled strength of 4,163, of whom 3,975 are efficients.

ACCIDENTS AT Rtmrcouar.—On Tuesday, James Fine- gan, of Salkeld-square, badly fractured 'his thumb whilst working at the Soap and Alkali Co.'s. On Monday, a driver in the employ of the Bridgewater Navigation Co., andnamed John Gibson, fractured his shoulder through a horse falling upon him. On Wednesday, a young married man named Wm. Burnham, of Fryer-street, who is employed at Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele's, was passing a lime well at the works during a temporary escape of steam, and fell with his left leg into the well, severely scalding it.

RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. On Thursday afternoon, an adjourned meeting of the Run- corn Board of Commissioners was held, for the purpose of closing the accounts for the financial year. Mr. George Marshall presided, and there were also present :—Messrs. Lyon, Norman, Frith, Taylor, J. J. Speakman, Steele, Han 1- ley, G. Hazlehurst, Timmins, Briscoe' McDougall, Meadow- croft, Brookes (secretary), and Barker (surveyor). The various accounts for the month, and including all up to the end of the financial year were formally proposed and passed by various members; and no discussion of any public in- terest arose upon them, the business being nearly of a purely formal character. It may be interesting to our readers to state that the estimates for the last financial year were as follows:—Finance, £1,507 ; General Purposes', £1,035; Canal Boats, £2O; and Highway and Sanitary Committee, £2,200; making a total of £4,762. The suns actually ex- pended was £4,718, or £44 less than the estimates, and was divided as under :—Finance Committee, £1,581 ; General Purposes, £1,099; Canal Boats, £l3 ; and Highway and Sanitary, £2,025.

SAD DEA.TEE OF A MAN AT WIDNES. —On Wednes- day, an inquest was held at the Britannia Inn, Irwell-street, Widnes, by Mr. C. E. Driffleld, county coroner, on the body of Patrick McGuire, a furnaceman, aged 38, of London-street who was found in the water near the Widnes locks, about half-past eleven, on Monday morning, by P.C. Roes. Mr. Bilsbrough, goods and canal agent to the London and North-Western Railway Co., was present to watch the pro- ceedings on their behalf. The witnesses examined were Rose McGuire, wife of deceased; Thomas Connolly, and P.C. Ross. The evidence showed that deceased appeared to have been at work on Sunday, and to have left about six o'clock in the evening. Instead of going home, he went to Wright's public-house, which is on the canal bank, and re- mained there until closing time. About ten at night, the witness Connolly was working in Messrs. Hutchinson's shed when the deceased, who appeared to be under the influence of drink, walked through the place as if on his way home. He asked him to wait until he got a light with which he could see him across the locks. He went for the light, but on his return he found that deceased had gone, and he was not seen again until his body was found in the canal. It is supposed that the poor fellow was going along the canal bank towards home, and fell into the water owing to his being under the influence of drink and the night being dark. Tj he ury returned an open verdict.

RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.—DEFEAT OF THE MINISTRY.—The proceedings began in a very tame manner on Tuesday evening, and to judge by the apathy Of the few members present and the almost empty benches in that portion of the house allotted to stranger, no one would have thought that before the house rose there would be any- thing approaching a scene or party tight. The amend- ments to the Licensing Bill were being discussed in com- mittee in a quiet manner, when It became evident that the Opposition benches were gradually filling. Heads were being counted by the leaders of both parties, which led to activity on the part of the Liberal whips. An amendment, moved by the Leader of the Opposition, was now before the com- mittee, and neither party cared to close the discussion. At lastothe fatal moment arrived, and a division was called for, when it was found that the Government had suffered a defeat, the numbers being for the amendment 27; against 24; majority against the Ministry, 3. Toe announcement was received with great cheers from the Opposition. The Premier then rose to move and report progress, in order that he might have time to consult his colleagues, several of whom were not in their places that night. This was opposed by the Leader of the Opposition who called upon the Ministry to resign. Several member on the ministerial side ridiculed the idea of resigning on an amendment in committee of such a trivial nature, as it did not affect the principle of the bill. Another division was taken, and the motion was again lost. The opposition then went in for a little amateur obstruc- tion, and the Leader of the Opposition moved the suspension of the standing orders to allow time to pass the bill through committee, and proposed that the time be extended to one o'clock in the morning. Whereupon two home- lovmg Liberals hurried out of the house, evidently not , relishing the idea of an " all night sitting." The motion was put to the house. The Foreign Secretary then moved "that the Speaker do now leave the chair." Another division was taken, and the resolution met with a simlar fate to the preceding ones. Before any other question was brought forward the Speaker ruled the business of the sit- ting at an end. The House rose at 10-30. The utmost ex- citement prevailed throughout. The motion of the member for Birkenhead on the Transvaal war, which is one of the orders of the day for next week, is to be taken as one of want of confidence in the Goverment. When the full strength of both parties is likely to be brought oat. The ConservatiVes number about 30, and the Liberals about 50, so that the Government have nothing to fear if their men ao their duty. It is probable that the Licensing Bill will be withdrawn in order to make way for the debate on the Transvaal war policy, Tuesday next being the last night of the session.

MEETING OF RUNCORN RATEPAYERS.—On Thursday evening, a meeting of Runcorn ratepayers, called by Mr, Lyon and Mr. William Handley, overseers of the poor, was held, first, for the purpose of nominating a list of overseers to be returned to the justices of the peace; secondly, to authorise the overseers to purchase an ordnance plan for the use of their office: thirdly, to nominate two fit and proper persons to fill the offices at assessor and collector of assessed taxes for the year 1881-2; fourthly, to appoint two auditors of the accounts of the Burial Board to the 25th instant, and fix a time for the audit of the accounts and fifthly, to ' appoint another meeting of the ratepayers at which the ' report of the auditors should be received. Mr. Lyon ' presided, and there were also present Messrs. William Hand- ; ley, Thomas Norman, Thomas Riley, John Gleave, Henry Coleburn, Thomas Stringfellow, John Lowe, John Lunt, John Timperley, and W. Sutton (assistant overseer). Before proceeding to the business of nominating the overseers, Mr. Norman moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Lyon, Mr. Handley, I and Sutton, and spoke in very eulogistic terms of the ' manner in which they had performed their duties, which had won the general commendation of the ratepayers. They I had proved, emphatically, the right man in the right place. (Hear, hear.)—The resolution was seconded by Mr. String- I fellow, and carried unanimously.—Nominations were then I taken for overseers, and Messrs. William Lyon, William Handley Thomas Norman, and William Whittaker were ' proposed as the names to be submitted to the magistrates.— Mr. Stringfellow moved, and Mr Norman seconded, a motion to the effect that an ordnance map anti acreage-book should be purchased for the use:of the overseers' office, at a total cost of £5 la—On the motion of Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. Stringfellow, Mr. John Simpson was nominated as assessor of assessed taxes.—Mr. Sutton then stated that, in consequence of the great increase in the rateable value of the parish, he found that he was unable to carry out the work of collecting the assessed taxes in a manner satisfactorily to him- self, as, owing to the increase of the work, he had sometimes to do two days' labour in one. He warmly thanked the ratepeyers for the treatment which he had always met with at their hands, and the manner in which his services bad been appreciated during the time he had held the office. He begged to suggest that Mr. Thomas Cooke, the assistant secretary of the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association, would be a very suitable person to nominate for the purpose of tilling the office. Mr. Cooke was a steady :young man, thoroughly trustworthy, and very industrious. In conclusion,' Mr. Sutton remarked that he should have pleasure in giving Mr. Cooke all the instruction he could as to the manner in which the duties had to be per- formed.-'-It was unanimously agreed that Mr. Cooke should be nominated for the office, on the proposition of Mr. Nor- man, seconded by Mr. Stringfellow.—Mr. Norman moved, and Mr. Stringfellow seconded the election of Mr. George Moss, as auditor of the Burial Board accounts; and Mr. Riley, and Mr. Bisbrown seconded Mr. Fairhurst. Both motions were carried. On the proposition of Mr. Norman, Seconded by Mr. Stringfellow, it was resolved that the audit should commence on the 11th inst.—On the proposal of Mr. Stringfellow, seconded by Mr. Daniel Bisbrown, it was agreed that the meeting ef ratepayers to receive the report )3hould be held on the 21st April, at seven in the evening.— A vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding concluded he proceedings.

WESTON RATEPAYERS' MEETING. On Thursday evening, a meeting of the ratepayers of Weston was held, at the Church school-room, for the follow- ing purposes:—To make out a list of persons to serve the office of overseers to be returned to the Justices of the Peace; to nominate two fit and proper persons to serve the office of Assessors of Land and Assessed Taxes for the year 1881.82. to take into consideration a resolution to be brought forward by Mr. Wm. Bankes, with regard to the recent legal pro- ceedings taken against him by the overseers for the recovery -of his Poor Rate; to consider and decide upon an applica- tion from the Assistant Overseer for an increase of salary, and to nominate a fit and proper person to serve the office of Waywarden. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also present the two overseers of the township, Messrs. Thomas Ford and John Poole; Messrs. James Handley, Thomas Handley, Wm. Guest, h. Rosenberg, J. W. Kirkham, Thomas Jeffs, John Beckett, James Ford, C. Ellis, E. Aaron, Captain Clarke, W. Rushes, J.P., and James Collier (assis- tant overseer). Messrs. Toomas Ford, John Poole, E. Aaron, and R. Clarke were nominated to serve the office of o,,erseer. Messrs. James Collier and James Ford were nominated to serve the office of assessors of land and assessed taxes. Mr. BANKES, J.P., objected to the course taken by the overseers with regard to the collection of spoor rate alleged to be due by him for land in Weston. In the first place,he was not the occupier of the land, but the owner. The occupiers of the land were Mr. Thomas Jeffs and Mr. Wm. Griffiths. The overseers thoroughly well knew that the land was so occupied, therefore they could not possibly excuse them- selves on the ground of ignorance. Yet they took legal proceedings against him for the recovery of the money. He gave them every information he possibly could, and informed them that owing to a dispute between the Alkali Company I and himself with respect to the tenancy, it was arranged' that the crops on the land were to be disposed of. The crops were sold for twelve months ending Feb., 1880, to Mr. Jeffs and Mr. Griffiths, with the distinct understanding that during that time they should pay all rates. On the 27th July, the taxes were paid by the tenants to the auctioneer. He had no right to receive them, but he paid them over to the assistant overseer. Mr. Bankes then proceeded to state the circumstances under which the second rate was alleged to be due by him, and said he considered he had been shamefully treated in the matter. He therefore begged to move "That the course taken by the overseers against my- self in respect of certain poor rates alleged to be due by me 18 occupier of land in the township of Weston, was unwar- rantable, and due to vindictive feeling on the part of the said overseers." Captain CLARKE regretted that the legal proceedings had to be taken, and said the matter ought to be fully investi- gated. He seconded the motion. Mr. AARON considered that Mr. Bankes was the person liable for payment of the rates of the land and not Messrs. Jeffs and Griffiths. Mr. BANLES said the land was re-let by the occupiers, and he had not received the slightest benefit from it. Mr. POOLE, one of the overseers, remarked that Mr. Baukes' name appeared on the rate-book as occupier, and that he as a magistrate signed the rate. The overseers strongly denied that the proceedings were taken through vindictive feeling. Mr. Poole then stated why legal pro- ceedings had been taken, and the trouble they had been put to in collecting the rate. They considered that in adopting the course they did they had only done their duty. They had not shown a vindictive spirit. To them the matter was a very unpleasant affair. A RATEPAYER, Mr. Dutton, at this point objected to the Presence of the reporter, saying that he was of opinion that he had no business there. • The CHAIRMAN said it would be contrary to all English proceedings to order a reporter out of the room. (Hear, hear.) Mr. DUTTON said he had known them to be expelled from a meeting of Guardians. • The CHAIRMAN said certainly no such thing had hap- pened since he had been chairman of the Runcorn Board of Guardians. Mr. Durron said he referred to Warrington. Captain CLARKE said as a body of Englishmen they would not object to the press reporting their proceed- ings. He was pleased to see a reporter present, and that they ought to be glad their meetin (Applause.) g was to be reported. Mr. Drrron then " closed up." Mr. Rasmus said he thought he might have signed the rate, he did so in a magisterial capacity. No one could ex- pect a magistrate when the rate book was brought to him, to go through it from beginning to end. Mr. COLLIER, assistant overseer, said Mr. Bankes signed the rate at his own house, and not at the court. Mr. BANICES differed with Mr. Collier, and remarked further that when Mr. Collier came for the poor rate of his own house he offered the money to him three times, but he refused to take it. Mr. COLLIER said it was contrary to all reason to supnose that he should refuse to take the money when it was offered to him. Mr. BANKES said he was positive that he was correct in what be stated. Mr. Collier refused to accept his own rate, without also receiving the amount demanded for the land. He said he would have all or none. Mr. THOMAS HANDLEY understood that the crops were sold; and the price paid included all rates. It was a question whether the money was paid to Mr. Bankes; because, if the whole of it was so paid, it included the rates, and so far as he could see, Mr. Backes was the person liable to pay the rates. (hear, hear.) Mr. BANILES stated that he had never received any money, and had not derived the slightest benefit. Mr. JAMES HANDLEY wished to know who instructed the auctioneers to sell the crops. Mr. Bankes stated that be was simply the owner of the land, and Mr. Aaron had stated that the auctioneers were employed by Mr. Bankes; consequently they were his servants. If Mr Banks did give instructions to the auctioneers, then the overseers could look to no one else for the money; they had nothing to do with the auctioneers. Mr. BANICES, in reply to Mr. Handley, stated the his solicitors employed the auctioneers, and he told them, as near as he could, the amount of the rates, to guide them. Mr. AARON asked Mr. Griffith, who was present, if he paid his rates to Mr. Bankes. Mr. GRIFFITHS said he paid nothing whatever to Mr. Bankes; what be did pay, he paid to the auctioneers. Mr. J. HANDLEY thought they could not look into the matter thoroughly until they had the conditions of sale. Mr. JAMES FORD regretted very much that the unpleasant- ness had arisen. They ceuld not gain much by it, but it would tend rather to estrange them from each other. They were all neighbours, and he would advise them te let the matter rest. After a few further remarks from Mr. POOLE, who stated that they took the proceedings on the advice of Mr. Henry Linaker, The CHAIRMAN said he agreed with what had been said by Mr. Ford, and if the matter was allowed to rest it ,would be very much better. Mr. BANICES said he was only aggrieved at the way in which he been treated, but he was now perfectly willing to with- draw his motion. Captain Clarke, as the seconder, also agreed to the with- drawal of the motion, and it was agreed to. Mr. J. HANDLEY said he bad hoped it would be under- stood that no reflection whatever was cast on the overseers. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN said he thought that was well under- stood.

div.head: ASSIST'A.NT OVERSEER AND HIS SALAHY.
div.p: THE ASSIST'A.NT OVERSEER AND HIS SALAHY.

The meeting next proceeded to consider an application of the Assistant Overseer for an increase of salary. He explained that the auditor had disallowed his travelling expenses, which, in the year, amounted to about £3 or £4. This amount be had had to pay out of his own pocket. It was agreed to increse his salary from £4O to £45 per annum. ROADS.
THE

Mr. J. W. KIRKHAM, Ch—e—reiiring-Waywarden, submitted a balance sheet, which showed that there was at the com- mencement of the year a balance of £3l 10s. ld. in favour of the township. The contribution during the past year had been £292, making a total amount in the hands of the authorities of £326 10s. id. The amount paid to the dis- trict or common fund war £172 9s. id., leaving a balance in favour of the township of £154.

A short discussion took place with regard to the bad state of the roads in several parts of the township, more particu- larly at Weston Point, during which several ratepayers spoke very strongly on the matter, and it was decided that the Daresbury Highway Board be requested to adopt cer- tain roads in the township, and that a deputation, consisting of Messrs. James Handley, Thomas Ford, E. Johnson, J. W. Kirkham, Thomas Jeffs, and Captain Clarke, be ap- pointed to represent the township at the next meeting of the Highway Board. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Kirkham for his ser- vices as waywarden.
THE QUESTION OF A SECOND GUARDIAN FOR THE TOWNSHIP.

The CHAIRMAN said in accordance with the wish e x- pressed at a previous township meeting he had written to the Local Government Board with reference to the appoint- ment of an additional guardian for Weston. He had re- ceived a reply stating that in view of the nearness of the annual electionit was inexpedient to make an alteration; and further that after the result of the approaching census had been made known it would be competent to make a fur- ther application for an alteration in the representation of the township.

On the motion of Captain CLARRE, seconded by Mr. J. HANDLEY, a vote of thanks was accorded to Canon Barclay for presiding, and the meeting further expressed a strong wish that he be re-appointed as the guardian for the town- ship of Weston.
THE POLICE DllPED.—Amongst the money paid in fines at the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, was a counterfeit halfcrown, which was not discovered until the person issuing it had gone away.

MAD DOG IT WARRINGTON. —On Tueaday evening, at about half-past five, much excitement was caused in the neighbourhood of Edgeworth-street by the presence of a mad dog. No danger was, however, to be apprehended, as the animal, a large black retriever, had been confined in the timber yard of Mr. John E. Wright, builder, around which a ,large crowd gathered. P.C. Neill arriving on the spot, the dog, by his orders,.was shot by a man named George Walton, n d at once buried No person or dog was, we understand, bitten by it.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. -

HOUSE OF LORDS. THE Thattsys.AL.—Earl KIMBERLEY, replying to Lord Bury, believed the massacre of the 94th was covered by the amnesty, but further information might arrive.—Earl CAIRNS gave notice that on Thursday he would call atten- tion to thb afrangement with the Boers, and ask for an ex- planation.—Lord KIMBERLEY, replying to Lord Larnington, said that suaerainty'hnplied less than sovereignty. England would retain the right to control the foreign relations of the Boers. Earl GRANVILLE corrected a mistake he had made about the holidays. They would be from Bth April to sth May. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. THE HIGHWAY ACT.—Mr. PEASE gave notice to move an amendment to the motion of Colonel Harcourt, to the effect that it was expedient to amend the Highway Act with rela- tion to main roads.

A DISTURBANCE BY SOLDIERS.—Me. FORSTER, replying to The O'Donoughue, slid on one occasion a party of six soldiers got drunk and created a disturbance in the streets of Castle Island, but there was no assault committed. The soldiers had been taken into custody, and they had been dealt with by the military authorities.—Mr. FORSTER said the officers of the Royal Irish Constabulary were not sub- ject to rules for compulsory retirement.—Mr. GRANT DUFF said the Government had come to a conclusion as to the establishment of State-aided emigration from the United Kingdom to the colonies. THE TRANSVAAL.—Mr.GrAnsrown said the arrangements come to to protect and compensate persons in the Transvaal for all acts not justified by the practice of civilised warfare would, the Government were advised, cover the massacre of Colonel Anstruther and the detachment of the 94th. Mr. Gladstone deferred answering the question as to the date of the commencement of the proceedings of the Commissioners at the Transvaal, ard the instructions.sent to them. until Monday. CANDAHAR.—The adjourned debate on Mr. STANHOPE'S motion condemning the withdrawal of British troops from Can,labar, was resumed.—Lord G. HAMILTON considered the step decided on by the Government most unwise, and opposed to-the highest military authority. He did not think he should have been able to vote for the perpetual occupation of Candahar, but he believed the mode and movement selected by the Government to carry out the withdrawal, without allowing the Indian Government time to make adequate preparations, unfortunate and unwise. He censured the Government for directing the evacuation of Candahar before they had taken steps to keep Russian influence from Afghanistan. The noble lord insisted that not suffi- cient steps had been taken to :counteract Russia's influence in Cabot, and concluded by denying that the present opposi- tion was conceived in a spirit of aggression or blood thirsti- ness. It was, he said, not carried en in a spirit of panic, but in the interests of homanitv. They objected to allow the foundltions of the Indian Empire to be sapped, or her bul- warks overthrown.—Mr. FAWCETT defended the Indian policy of the Government, and said the Liberal party was united in their desire to see that policy carried out with courage and firmness. He thought the penalties they were paying for annexations were quite sufficient to justify them in withdrawing from Candahar, and as the people of Afghanistan were lovers of independence it would not be sound policy to act in opposi- tion to that feeling. He did not think the promise made to the people of Afghanistan, that there should be no annexa- tion of territory, except for purposes of defence would be kept, if Candahar, one of its provinces, was retained. Wrong, once done, he said ought notjto be repeated, and injustice once committed ought speedily be redressed.— Mr. ONSLOW supported the motion. He though: Russian influence ought to be extinguished in Afghanistan, and, referring to the Cabul troops sent by Abdul Rahman to Can- dahar, he thought the 5,000 men would be totally inadequate to meet the large army that Ayoob Khan would shortly bring against the place.—Mr. Bum did not believe that our withdrawing from Candahar would induce Russia to advance. Neither did he think it would diminish the prestige of England in India.—Mr. DALRYMPLE supported the motion, and pointed out that Sir Donald Stewart could no longer be quoted as an authority in favour of retirement. div.head: WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

. ANNUAL MEETING. The Widnes Liberal Association held their annual busi- ness meeting last evening, in the Widnes Hall. Mr. E. K. Muspratt, the president, eccupied-the chair. The annual report having been reed by Mr. Shores, the Chairman reviewed the work done by the association during the past year, and said that although the polling resulted in the return of two Tories for that division of the county, still he was persuaded—and bethought that most of them must he persuaded—that, oft the whole, Widnes did its duty. He criticised at length the statenient put forth by the Con- servatives, and said he could not understand how a working- man could be a Conservative, which was a very different thing from saying that there was no such thing in existence as a Conservative workingman; for they knew that working- men were only men after all, and there were a certain number of men who had not minds of their own. In fact, some people, speaking ef these sort of people, and using not very polite language, would say that they were fools. Cer- tainly, if a workingman wanted to remain in one condition all his life; if he wanted his wages to remain at the same low rate; if he did not want improvement and reform, he was an extraordinary creature ; but, at the same time, he had not the slightest doubt that such ' people did exist amongst the working classes, and there was equally little doubt that they joined Conservative Associations, and were termed "Conservative workingmen." The speaker then referr4l to the actions of the late Govern- ment and also to those of Mr. Gladstone, approving of his foreign policy. He concluded by hoping the Government would not permit their Land Bill to be emasculated and mutilated by the House of Lords; and moving the adoption of the report. Mr. MARTIN TAYLOR seconded the motion, and said that when they scratched a Tory workingman, and -got below the skin, they were sure to find a Republican. He severely criticised the figures quoted at the Conservative meeting, and said he was quite willing to meet Major Cross to enquire into the matter. tie strongly condemned the alle- gation made by the President of the Ccnservative Associa- tion as to what Mr. Gladstone was stated to have said in his Midlothian speeches, but he supposed that gentleman had only repeated the parrot-like statement of the Tory press on the subject. The resolution was carried unanimously. On the proposition of Mr. MARTIN TAYLOR, seconded by Mr. PANKHURST, the President and Vice-President were ap- pointed delegates to the Executive Committee of the South- West Lancashire Liberal Association. Mr. Kidd and Mr. Joseph Robinson were appointed auditors, on the motion of Mr. SIDNEY Mrsmarr and Mr. W. BERRINGTON JONES.. .
• Tho proceedings terminated with a resolution expressive of approval at the action of lier:Majesty's Government in regard•to the Transvaal and Afghanistan.

A WIDNES MAN DROWNED IN THE MERSeY.—Mr. Clarke Aspinall, coroner for Liverpool, held an inquest yesterday on the body of Joseph Once, 48, labourer, who resided at 43, Wellington-street, Widnes. Deceased joined the flat Trial as an extra hand on Sunday night, and on the voyage to Liverpool the flat encountered rough weather, and went down in the river a little to the north ef Garston. Deceased and the others on board the flat got into a punt, which was swamped, and its occupants were thrown into the water. When deceased was rescued he was in an unconscious con- dition, but slightly recovered after being taken on hoard the tug Gladiator. He was conveyed to the Northern Hospital, where he died on Thursday from pi eu nonia, the result of immersion. The jury found a verdict accordingly.

FAIR AT PRESTON. At the second annual cheese fair held at Presto, day, nine dairies were pitched in competition for t. poration prizes, and in nine others the produce was for ranging from 4 to 18 cwt. each. For cheese from far. under 100 acres the first prize was awarded to Cowell, o. Goosnargh ; 2nd, Riding, Goodplumpton ; 3rd, Salthouse, Roseacre. Over 100 acres: Ist, Bailey, Goosnargh ; 2nd, Hull, Bibby Hall; 3rd. Bradley, Little Marton. There was a much larger and better show than last year, and the prices asked ranged from 755. te 90s. There has been a very boisterous night.

div.head: I SPORTSMAN IN TROUBLE.
div.p: I SPORTSMAN IN TROUBLE.

Yesterday the Barnsley magistrates fined Arthur Elliott, clerk, residing at Manchester, 20s. and costs, for travelling on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway, at Penistone, without a ticket, on Thursday. Defendant, who was found under the carriage seat without a ticket, said he had been to Lincoln races and lost all his money. It was stated that four similar cases were pending at Ashton and six at Warrington. THE GALE: COMMUNICATION INTERRUPTED.

• A full and strong gale blew off Liverpool, yesterday, ao- cornpanied by rain squalls. Tke direction of the wind was W.N.W. The sea was also very rough. Communicatiol with the outports was inierrupted during the whole of the morning, and consequently it is not known if any disasters have occurred. Coasting steamers arriving arriving in the Mersey report the prevalence of exceptionally heavy weather outside. Shipping generally is being much inconvenienced by the adverse weather which has prevailed within the last few days, and more than one steamer which sailed from the river a day or two ago is still at anchor but a short distance outside the port. On the river the wind was blowing with much violence, but no casualties are reported. The severe storm in the north had somewhat abated yee- terday. Yesterday morning the Highland Railway mail steamer John o'Groats, Kirkwall to Thurso, drifted on to the rocks at Scrabster Pier. All efforts to get her off have proved unavailable, but the cargo has been saved.
TILE ATTEMPT TOHBOIC. UP THE MANSION

-- -- The LOndon prince, in conjunction with the Government, have offered a reward of £3OO for the apprehension of Thomas Mooney, a bricklayer, aged twenty-eight or thirty O'Donnell, aged thirty-two, who has been in America; and John Coleman, known as Pat Coleman, a waiter, aged thirty; all of whom are suspected of being concerned in the attempt to blow up the Mansion House. A free pardon and £lOO reward is offered to accomplices.

FrbERATION OF OPERATIVE POTTERS. The operatives of the various branches employed in the Staffordshire potteries having withdrawn from the Board of Arbitration, in consequence of dissatisfaction with the award in the last arbitration before Mr. Brassey, M.l'., a meeting was held at Tunstall on Wednesday night to inaugurate the formation of a federatinn of workmen, with a view to united action for the recovery of their losses. A resolution was unanimously carried that annual hiring should take place at Midsummer instead of Martinmas. One branch was stated to have decided to establish a co-operative manufactory. A CLEROYMAN COMMITTED TOR TRIAL.

------- The Rev. Thomas Howard Twist, vicar of St. Michael's, Derby, has been committed for trial by the Derby magistrates for fraudulently intercepting and detaining two telegrams sent to the superintendent of police by a firm of London solicitors. Tbe defendant also sent tictitioua telegrams to London'. He admitted the facts alleged. SERIOUS FIRE AT NICE.

A are, disastrous in its results, took place at the Hallam Opera House in Nice, on Wednesday night, owing to an ex- plosion of gas. Many lives were lost, 59 bodies having been taken out of the ruins by three o'clock on Thursday morning.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

LIVERPOOL COTTON.—Spot: With a weak market only a small buginess has been done, and quotations are barely main- tained. Sales 7000 bales, including 500 on speculation or for export. The sales for the week are 43380 bales, erne more than the estimate. Spinners have taken 59650 bales. including 19310 bales forwarded direct. The import is 124897 bales, and the ex- port 3520 bales. The steel( has increased 62730 bales. The visible supply is 612,550 bales more than at the same time last year. MANCHESTER COTTON.—The market opened flat, and a little easier where there was anything to afford an indiedion. There was no fresh news from any quarter, but the tone of all cotton reports, and particularly of unofficial reports, was adverse, and had its effect. .7•••••••*,,..--, -. ..... _ THE LAND QUESTION. I noticed in The Examiner of the 12th init. a very able diet nn the land question, signed "H. W.," and also a reply signed "J.," in The Examiner of the 19th. As this is one of the most important questions now occupying the public mind, I think it is necessary that facts should be quoted, and sot brag and bluster. "J," in his reply, says I baye read the vapour, ificc., of 'H. W.'" I think, sir, that the letter of Illlr. was a very able one, and consisted of farts perhaps * genial to your correspondent "J.," for he does not deal he all-important question, viz., the land question. Let briefly what is meant by this question. Now, sir, I the right and proper end of all government in every Itn, political community should be to bring about, if possible, tlen greatest happiness to the greatest number, and this can- not be where a few thousand families are living in luxury splendour • whilst millions of useful and toiling sub- are without the comforts ant the necessaries of rife. either pauperism nor excessive wealth are things to be desired, for ooth are the parents of private vice. Agur prayed "Give me neither poverty nor riches, feed me with food- convenient fcr my use, lest I be full and deny Thee and say, Who is the Lord? Or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain." It is generally admit- ted that land is the source of all wealth, and the laws which regulate this and consequently affect the root of happiness are therefore of the highest importance. What are these laws, and what effect do they produce? Up to the Norman invasion, land, on the death of its owner, passed to his children in equal shares. William the Coaqueror brought with him the feudal laws then prevailing on the continent, the basis of which was that all land was helddirectly or in- directly from the King. The King granted what he did not hold to lords of the manor, on certain rents or services— chiefly military service—and the lords in their turn made grants to tenants, who rendered payments in kind, military or domestic service. The greatest service rendered to the King in those turbulent days was the military service, and on the death of lord Gr tenant, all land, dm., should pass to the eldest son (who might reasonably be supposed the moet likely to render such service), to the exclusion of younger sons and daughters. This is the simple origin of our pre- sent law, that freehold or copyhold property, in the absence of a will, descends to the eldest son, to the exclusion of his brothers and sisters, or, in other word, the law of primogeni- ture. [ think it is obvious that the preference forth. eldest son is grossly unjust to the younger members of the family; and what is unjust to them is injurious to the com- munity. Let us see how the land is chiefly held. The total area of the United Kingdom is 72,000,000 acres. Of this, 10,000,000 are held by 51,000 persons,holding between 100 and 1,000 acres; and 10.888 persons hold over 1,000 acres each, or altogether 51,885,000 acres. But we will go higher still, and take those who own more than 5,000 each, and we have the startling fact that 2,184 individuals hold altogether 38,875,522 acres, or 2,815,542 acres more than half the area of the United Kingdom, excluding the metro- polis; and from that number may be culled 421 persons who hold 22.880,755 acres, or 4,8-50,765 acres—more than a fourth part of the whole kingdom. lilt be true that land is the source of all wealth, and that wealth, more or less, is essential to happiness, and that a just Government should seek the happiness of the greatest number, it is impossible to argue that it is just to maintain laws which practically convey all the land of the country to 200,000 people, leaving nearly 32.000,000 without an inch of it, and which practi- cally convey to 2,184 persons more than half of the kingdom and much more than a fourth of it to 421 men. What is the natural consequence of excessive wealth, but idleness. Luxury, vice, and ill- example in waste and extravagance to all classes below. Ye friends to truth, ye statesmen who survey The rich man's joys increase, the poor's decay. 'Tis yours to judge how wide the limits stand Between a splendid and a happy land. And when we compare this country to any other continental nation, we must not forget the great advantages we enjoy. Our insular position makes us practically safe from invasion. We do not live in fortified towns, our cities burned and our country ravaged by hostile troops, as they too often do. Our soil is fertile, our climate temperate, our mines are 1 :menses of great wealth. We are distinguished for our energy and spirit of entcrprise, and everyone will admit we are both industrious and laborious. And if, in spite of all these advantages, we find drunkenness, extravagance, rags, pauperism, and crime, it is certainly worth while to seek the cause. I believe th,t primogeniture, settlement, and entail is reeponsible for very much of it. Property gives a man self-respect. It has a desire to increase and make its owner thrifty, sober, and acts as a security against adversity, and gives him a stake in society, and a direst interest in the good government of the country. In every way it has a powerful influence on mind and con- duct ; but the want of property among the masses of the people is accompanied by a general want of prudence, and of influences to counteract the improvidence of men in hopelees circumstances. People living without means or prospect of improving their condition have no motives to exert foresight or economy, and no class is so reckless as that which lives to-day upon the labour of yesterday. And it is not in hnman nature that they will permit the present miner/nal distribution of the land—caused, be it remembered,l net by nature or Providence, but by unwise and barbarous laws—long to continue. Let us willingly remove the senses el the mischief, and abolish the law of primogeni- ture, settlement, and entail. Then, without doing wrong to any man or to any family, a mighty change for good would gradually come over the country, and we should peacefully approach that happy time when every man shall at in safety under his own vine what he plants, and sing Ile merry song of peace to all his neighbours.--I am, Sir, truly yours, JOHN SHUFFLEBOTHAM.

OUR HEREDITARY PAUPERS. Sir,—lt seems we have one in our midst who thinks right to defend perpetual pensions, that is, that the hard earnings ef the people should swell the already large in-. comes of those who do not earn their livings by the sweat of their brow. Two names are thrust before as, each having its origin in a fighting man. The first, that of Churchill, being a descendant of John Churchill, the eon of a•needy Danger-on at the court of Charles IL John had a sister, Arabella, maid to the Duchess of York, who being seduced by the Duke. was the means of John's rapid promotion in Ike army. John Churchill was presented with £5,000 by She Mildest; of Cleveland, as a reward for his activity in leaping ftut of the window when the King surprised the pretty pair under suspicious circumstances. Macauly speaks of him as a man who owed his rise to his sister's dishonour. By the time he was thirty-seven years of age, Chnrehill,throngh the Duke of York's influence, had be- come a major-general and a peer of both England and Scotland, and held several well-paid offices. After publicly vowing; that he would spend the last drop of his blood in the service of James 11., he began to plot against him, and although trusted implicitly and promoted to the office of lieutenant- general he basely deserted him, and pas treacherous enough to leayz the council of war which had been protracted to a late hoar in the night, and before morning be in the camp of the enemy William of Orange. He was rewarded for this, ao William created him Earl of Marlborough. But here again Churchill was true to his nature, because for treason to William he was dismissed from office and confined in the tower. At William's death, Marlborough, through the in- !hence of his wife, rose to the highest pinnacle of power, the queen created him a duke, and conferred upon him an annual pension of £5,000 out of the post office revenues. The queen also offered to the duchess £2,000 a year from her privy purse, which was declined at the time, but nine years after, when the queen and the duchess had quarrelled, the letter claimed and received the whole of the arrears. Soon after the splendid victory of Blenheim dazzled the House of I Commons, and he was at once rewarded with the royal manor and honour of Woodstock, and the hundred of Wooton, —formerly ancient lands of the crown,—and half a million was expended in building a palace and removing encum- brances on the estate. After the battle of Ramilies a pension e £4,000 a year was settled upon him and his heirs for ever, the gross amount paid to the present time is £664,000. /30 much for the Marlborough pensio Is it to continue for over? Has Parliament a right to tax posterity, so that generals may be rewarded in this outrageous fashion? A Matthew Mattical writer sheds forth this bright idea : " Once admit the principle that hereditary pensions are to be abolished, or even forcibly commuted at anything less than market value, and the floodgates of Communism are opened." lam no Communist, but I soon should be if I thought it would tend to make the poor richer and the rich poorer. But let me say a few more words respecting this illustrious pauper family. Loud complaints were made in the House of Com- mons of Marlborough's greediness and dishonesty. It was alleged that the Duke had received in ten years £63,000 from bread contractors in the army; and further, that he lad received 2/ per cent. on the pay of the foreign troops pubsidized by England, and the House of Commons censured his conduct. At the time when Marlborough was secretly tetteiving large sums from army contractors he and the Duchess held offices and emoluments of the annual value of 21114,3e5. Marlborough House, Pall Mall, cost the nation 00,000. The Churchill family have at various times re- ceived out-door relief from the national revenues, in addition to the hereditary annual pension. Their motto " Faithful but unfortunate." I think honest folk will have but one opinion respecting the above. The next illustrious name is now held by one who is famous fie takingthe chair at religious meetings and nothing else. liord Nelson, a name dear to the hearts of Englishmen, whether war is to be deprecated or not we need not now &muss, but I may quote Lord Derby as to the feeling that exists amongst the upper classes. Speaking at Rochdale, be says, "There is scarcely a family in the upper classes that has not some connection with the army. It is a mere delusion to say that everybody is against war. On the contrary, there are a good many persons who either think that they will make a very good thing out of a war, or that they willeerve to keep off something that they dislike even more." These rewards must have a highly stimulating effect npott those who have any hopes of obtaining glory of that description. William Wilberforce, speaking of the Nelson grant and pension, said he viewed the matter as a pledge of national liberality to encourage imitation, and it is for this reason that I strongly condemn giving the Ration's money to trained fighting men. In 1797 Nelson was awarded a pension of £l,OOO per annum. In the follow- ing year he was awarded further pensions of £l,OOO by the Irish Parliament, and £2,000 by the English. At his death the £2,000 pension was continued to his childless widow. The East India Company presented him with £lO,OOO. Soon after Nelson's death it was proposed on behalf of the Government that a sum of £120,000 should be vested in trustees, of which mOOO was to be given to each of Rieloon's two sisters, £lO,OOO to Nelson's brother—a clergy-

man, a servant of the prince of Peace, aho was created an earl—er his brother's daughter, and £90,000 to be expended' in the purchase of an estate for the holders of the Nelson peerage. Further, a perpetual pension of £5,000 per annum was annexed to the peerage, to enable its holder to support the dignity of an earl. Thus we ses that collateral rela- tives, whose ancestors never did anything for the nation, are most dishonestly living on the nation. The total amount received by the Nelson family is £571,000. Sir, an unscru- pulous neutral dares to cry out "Communism," because Mr. Bradlaugh wishes to rid the country of these paupers. I say he deserves all praise. and the man who makes it pos- sible for his fellow man to lead a honest life is not to be sneered at.—Yours, H. W. P.S.—lf your correspondent, "$." thinks I wish to take his rand or his hard earnings from him, he is much mis- taken. Communism, as generally understood, I dislike. I hope I respect property and its rights; but I see no rights of property in such cases as I have sketched above. Respect- ing the land tax, I need not descend to calling names, for it does no good, and therefore it is a mere waste of time. i When William Pitt, n 1793, accepted the valuation of 1692, he said .that his measure for the nominal land tax of 45 in the pound was not intended to prevent a future Parliament from augmenting that tax. The land tax to-day is at a ridiculous low figure. Entirely omitting the value of minerals, Sze., the highest land tax paid is in Suffolk, 51-d. in the pound. In many counties the tax is i less thaa Id. in the pousd, and in some less than one farthing n the pound. In Lancashire the land tax is half a farthing in the pound, and in Scotland three- sixteenths of a penny. The general average of the land tax throughout the United Kingdom is a penny and five-eighths of a penny per pound. This may ho vapour. If so, it is of such a dense character that the people will not be able to bear it much longer. H. W.
Sergeant

COAL AT FRODSHAM. Sir,—Seeing in your paper statements every week in refer- ; ence to the coal trade, I would like to make a few remarks ' in connection with that trade at Frodsham station. Before 1 the strike of the colliers (which I think was most justifiable) we had a fair quality of coal delivered at 9s. 2d. per ton, the best, if I remember right, being about 12s. 6d, per ton. In consequence of the strike we were quickly informed that coal was dearer and for common coal we had to pay 15s. 10d. per ton, it being much inferior in quality to what we had before the strike at 9s. 2d. per ton. When the strike in a great measure ended, we expected to have coal cheaper, and our expectations were, last week, realised, for the vendors of this useful commodity lowered the price one halfpenny per cwt.; rather a large sum, especially as they tell their cus- tomers it is not them that causes coal to be so clear, and I have never yet (during the strike) seen a report ii any paper which says that colliers are getting ss. 101 per ton more than they were getting before the strike, neither are they getting it now. So, Mr. Editor, I consider this is anything but right. The colliers are not getting this extra cash, we know the sellers here say they are not getting it; I would like to know who is. If it is the masters, I think the colliers had better strike again; not a few, but every one through- out England, Scotland, and Wales. But I cannot think it is the masters for this reason: at Delamere station, 6 miles from here, coal is much cheaper; common coal is only 6d. and the very best,but 'lid. per cwt., at the present time. This means no less than 4s. 2d. per ton, to which may be added 10d., as the freight is 10d. per ton more to Delamere than to Frodsham. Now if this is not what an honest man tally rightly call an imposition, I have done. Sir, I would suggest that some enterprising coal agent should take up the matter and supply the public of Frodsham and neigh- bourhood with coal at a reasonable profit and I have no doubt he would soon reap the benefit; and then the sellers at Frodsham would not be quire so quick in saying that those who sold coal at Delamere were not all of one mind, though they are all of one mind at Frodsham. Hoping you will find space in your next issue for these remarks, I remain, yours, A SUFFERER. Frodsham, March 24th, 1881.

WARRINGTON POLICE CASES. MONDAY . Before Alderman Pickmere (Mayor) and Councillor Fa irclough. DESERTING HIS CRILDREN.—M i Ch a?.l Higgins was charged with unlawfully running away from the borough of Warrington on the 23rd February, leaving two children chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union. —Mr. Garnett, the relieving officer, said the cost of main- tenance had been .£1 18s 61—Prisoner was fined 40s and costs, or in default one month. t ASSAULT ON A Wwz.—John Rourke, a labourer, was charged with assaulting Margaret Rourke, his wife, on the 17th inst.—Prisoner on that day, at noon, went home and abused his wife. In the evening he again assaulted tier, striking her on the head and face in a most furious manner. —Prosecutrix, who appeared to have been roughly handled. said she did not want her husband to be sent to prison, as she would then have to apply for relief.—The Mayor: Can you live without him for a month? Prosecutrix : No, sir.— Prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for six months, or in default a month's bard labour. OFFENCE AGAINST THE FACTORY ACT—John Clough, master fustian cutter, Tanner's-lane, was summoned for em- ploying. on the sth March, Mary Ann Mullinger, contrary to the Factory and Workshops Regulation Act. He was also charged with illegally employing Ellen Fernley Mar. goret Richardson, Elizabeth Lang, and Mary Ann Cheshire. Defendant pleaded not guilty.—Captain W. Meade-King, H.M. inspector of factories, said he was sorry to be obliged i to appear before the Bench again, after so short an I interval, to ask their aid in stopping offences against' the Factory Act, which appeared to be becoming more pre-1 valent—he meant the allowing of women and young persons I to work at all hours of the night in what were known as fustian cutting shops in Warrington. The master cutters appeared to be of opinion that they had only to keep out of the way and allow young persons to act with impunity. It would be shown that in the present instance five females were at work in the defendans's cutting shop at about four o'clock in the morning. The earliest hour at which they could legally be employed would be six o'clock.—lnspector Profitt said that at four o'clock on Saturday morning, the sth inst , he was in Tanner's-lane, and he saw a light in defendant's cutting shop, and several persons working. He got thl assistance of P.S. Cox, and knocked at the door several times. It was opened by a woman named Mary Ann Mullinger, who stated, in answer to his inquiries, that there were five persons at work. The officers entered and found four girls, whose ages ranged from 15 to 19 years, at work. Mullinger re-commenced work whilst witness was there. She said, " We came about half-past three o'clock, and Mr. Clough don't know that we are working. I locked the shop up last night, and took the key borne with me."—P.S. Cox gave corroborative evidence.—Captain Meade King referred to sections 92 and 94 of the Factory and Workshops Act to show that it was the duty of the occupier of the premises to see that their workpeople did not work at improper hours, and that it was not sufficient for them to go away and allow their hands to keep the key. They must under- stand that certain responsibilities attached to them when they became employers of labour.—Defendant said he was Poorly at the time, and left Mary Ann Mullinger in charge. —Mr. White : She was constituted your foreman then.— Mary Ann Mullinger, called, said she got orders to lock the shop up and take the keys to the defendant's house, but she kept them so that they could go a little earlier the following morning. They thought they would go about 5-30, but when they got there it was only four o'clock. —lnspector Proffit and another constable said they had seen lights in the defendant's shop at four o'clock on many mornings previous to this occurrence.—The Mayor : We are obliged to administer the law. You are responsible for having your works open only at the proper hours, and you must pay 10s. and costs in each case. I think you may consider yourself very well let off. FRlDAY.—Before &aptain Reynolds and Mr. Ziba . Armitage. TROUBLESOME APPRENTICES.—EIizabeth Higgs was sum- moned by Mr. John Platt, fustian cutter, to show cause why she should not be committed to prison for neglecting her work.—The case was adjourned a month ago to give her a , chance of fulfilling her contract, but she had attended very irregularly, not having been at her work during the last andinthet tears, said mwoetuhlear seoef ththaet shdee f ewnednatn,t, was again adjourned for a month.—Pliza Burke was similarly summoned and committed to prison for seven days.—Thomas Lee was summoned by Mr. George Aspy for not fulfilling his contract. He had left the town and taken up the trade of a hawker. He was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment. moned by Margaret Tickle for using, on the 22nd instant, PROVOKING LANGUAGE.—Catinnine Hardman was sum- language calculated to provoke a breach of the peace.— Complainant said defendant had called her husband a " madman " and was creating ill-feeling between herself and her husband.—The case was dismissed. AN ARTFUL DonGEn.—Margaret Rourke, a middle-aged woman, was summoned for assaulting Nancy Smith, up- wards of 80 years of age, on the 17th instant.—Defendant, who looked very ill, exhibited signs of fainting, but a few sharp words from Mr. Hunt, who said the woman did the same every time she appeared, "brought her round."—Com- plainant stated that on the day in question, whilst she was at her own door, defendant without any provocation what- ever struck her on the face and blacked her eye.—Defendant said her husband was at the time " licking " her, and she' was striking him when the complainant came in the way, and the blow struck her.—She was ordered to pay the costs, 7s. 6d. CRUELTY TO A. Hons.—Mary Murphy was charged with unlawfully and cruelly illtreating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state, on Monday, the 16th instant.— Defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr. Luckings, inspector to the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, said that on the day named he was in the Warrington Market, when he saw a brown horse attached to a cart laden with potatoes. The animal was flinching, and appeared very uneasy. He examined it, and found under the pad an old wound as large as the palm of his hand, very deep, and extending to the bone. A quantity of Fuller's earth had been placed on the wound, but the matter had oozed through and was adhering to the pad.—Defendant said she was a widow, and had a large family to keep.—Captain Reynolds: That is no reason why you should illtreat the horse.—Defendant, on promising not to work the horse until the wound was healed, was ordered to pay the costs.

A curious subsidence took place in Whittle&ld on Mon- I day. A new shed has been recently built in the rear of Garstang-street, and opposite to this the foundation of a street of new houses has been laid. Between the engine house and the promised new houses, about 20 yards in length and 12 yards in breadth, the street has gone down at least six feet, dragging part of the engine house with it. It is supposed that there is an old pit underneath. The im- mediate neighbourhood is thickly populated. Mr. Broadhurst p-oposes to introduce, either in the Cor- rupt Practices Bill or in the Ballot Bill, a clause proyiding that the expenses of the returning officer shall bepaid out of the local rates. The clause is identical with one that was introduced into the Ballot Act of 1871. It passed the House of Lords, but was struck out when the Bill returned to the Commons. The principle is also embodied in a bill intro- duced this session by Mr. Ashton Mike. '—n origin
