Bd., and with intent to defraud the company. Prisoner pleaded guilty. A ticket collector said the prisoner arrived at Warrington by the 9.10 train on Wednesday night. He was discovered under the seat of the carriage, and had neither ticket nor money to pay his fare. Mr. Hunt said the Lincoln and Aintree races were on at this time, and extra provision was made at the station in the way of police and special inspec- tors as these attempts were very frequent. There were a good many pounds taken from characters like the prisoner who had tried to get to Liverpool without paying their fare. They were allowed to go on if they paid theinfare, but no one would pay for the prisoner. Prisoner, in answer to Captain Litton, said he kelonged to Leeds.—Captain Litton: I suppose you were going to see the Grand National to-morrow? No, sir. Prisoner was fined 40s. and costs, or in default one month's imprisonment.—Henry Peel pleaded 1 guilty to a similar charge. He was also found under the seat. Captain Litton : Where do you live ? Prisoner : Anywhere. I should have had my fare paid but they would not take it. The ticket collector said several of the pas station master, - sengers offered to pay the fare. Mr. Rigby, _ remarked that the other men were in league with the prisoner, and if he happened to be detected they would then pay his fare. Under such circumstances the company would Capt. not take the fare, as there was an intention to defraud. apt . Litton: I cannot but think that the Railway Company are bad judges in refusing to take the money. It would do them much more good than sending the man to prison. They take it from other people regularly. It is absurd. Mr. Hunt, didn't you say that they had received the fare from , other persons ? Mr. Hunt: But you see the train was in ' motion rhen they offered to pay for this man. Prisoner stated the train had not left the station when he was taken Into the street. Councillor Milner said there was the intent to defraud. Captain Litton (to prisoner) : There is no doubt about your attempting to defraud, but if the Railway Company had taken the money instead of bringing you here, it would have been wiser discretion. Prisoner was fined 20s. including costs, or, in default, 14 days' imprison- ' ment.—A similar charge was made against George Smith, who pleaded not guilty. He was "rolled up like :football" under the seat, and well screened by the large number of persons who were in the compartment. Prisoner said his home was at Shields, but be had gone to Lincoln to get work. He was not going to the races. Prisoner was fined 403. and costs, or one month. Prisoner: Thank you, sir. VAGRANTS—DanieI Cowen and Lamia Howard were charged with being vagrants, having been found in a closet in Rose and Crown-street, at half-past twelve this morning. —Mr. Runt said the female prisoner was the daughter of a very respectable man, but of late years she had gone sadly wrong.—Prisoners were discharged on promising .to leave the town.

REPLIES. The IRISH SECRETARY, replying to the member for Bel- fast, said the conduct of the hon. member, Mr. Parnell, had been under the consideration of the Government for some time, but it had not yet been decided to remove his name from the commission of the peace. (Hear, bear.) The COLONIAL SECRETARY stated, in answer to the mem- ber for Norwich, that the Government had heard with deep regret of the report of the proceedings of the Blantyre mis- sion, which, if true, reflected very gravely upon the mis- sionaries. (Hear, hear.) No effort would be wanting to elucidate the whole matter, and to bring to speedy justice such persons as were amenable to law. . (Hear, hear.) In reply to the member for East Cheshire, the PRIME MINISTER said: In the opinion of the Government it would be exceedingly unwise for the English to evacuate Candahar. (Ministerial cheers.) The LEADER of the OPPOSITION gave notice thathe would ask whether it was the intention of Her Majesty's Govern- ment to propose that England should bear the expense of the occupation of Candahar. (Opposition cheers.) The PRIME MINISTER, in answer to the member for Col- chester' who asked whether overtures for peace were first made by England or the Boers, said he need hardly say that no Cabinet of which he was a member would think of recom- mending that the English should sue for peace after suffer- ing three successive defeats. (Ministerial cheers.) The member for BANDON asked if the Government would introduce a scheme for the reformation of reforma- tories, and • The HOME SECRETARY, in reply, said he was afraid the anxiety of hon. members opposite to get into office would Prevent him bringing forward any of the measures mentioned in the Queen's speech. (" Oh.") THE ASSASSINATION OF THE RUSSIAN EMPEROR. The PRIME MINISTER said he thought the House should take notice of an event which took place a short time ago in Europe, and which made an impression upon the civilised world, and he proposed that an address be sent to the Queen and the Duke and Dechess of Edinburgh, sympathis- ing with them in their bereavement. The LEADER Of the OPPOSITION with all his heart seconded the vote of condolence to the Queen upon the very shockisg and painful event which had deprived Russia of an emperor. (Hear, hear.) The address was agreed to. THE LICENSING ACTS AMENDMENT BILL,—DEFRAT OF TES GOVERNMENT. The COLONIAL SECRETARY, in resuming the debate upon the Licensing Acts amendment Bill, said the debate must have indicated to a dispassionate observer that the right hon. member for Stroud had adopted a course of action which did not, he felt sure, commend itself to his inner consciousness (" Oh "); but that he had been driven to it by the clamour of a large section of his party ("Oh ") who, holding views of an extreme character, were never satisfied without pressing upon the house the consideration of legislative measures which had a tendency to increase and foment the discontent of all classes of society (" Oh "). The bill introduced by the right hon. gentleman at the head of the government dealt fairly and equitably with the question of Sunday closing, and it was a measure that was drawn up with moderation and having consideration for all those likely to be affected by its provisions. A large section of the members opposite were not content to let moderation be known unto all men—(laughter)—or rather to let their moderation be known unto all men. (Cheers.) On the contrary, their im- moderate desires were shown by the captious opposition to the bill before the house, and the pressure brought to hear upon the government by bringing forward a resolution as to legislation for Ireland. No one regretted more than the government the state of Ireland, and a bill had already been brought in, which met with the approval and acceptance of the house, which in its operation would deal vigorously and successfully with those who had largely contributed to produce the disorder, discontent, and crime which had ex- isted in that country. The Leader of the Opposition and the right hon member for Norwich had taunted the government with wasting the time of the house, but they forgot that on going out of office they left the government a legacy of in- creased troubles (loud laughter); that their vacilating and peace-at-any-price policy (" No, no," and cheers) had re- sulted in materially increasing their responsibilities and troubles in South Africa—(hear, hear)—in their utter confusion in the east, and in a general feeling of discontent and disorder in their colonial dependencies. If the hands of the government were to be forced at the instigation of a body of men who were unscrupulous as to the means they used to obtain their object, it would afford a precedent not likely to conduce to the interests and welfare of the country. The bill before the house was a step towards minimising an evil which in the opinion of all thoughtful men was the curse of this age. (Hear, hear.) Its adoption would be to ensure legislation which would have for its object the wel- fare and material prosperity of England, and it was quite as important in its urgency as any legislation having for its object the reformation of the land laws. He stated that he did not believe in sensational legislation, and whatever the result of the bill was their consciences would approve their desires and conduct. (Applause.) The right hen. member for NORTHAMPTON made a direct charge against the Government. In the speech issued at the opening of parliament the house were told that the ministry might introduce a measure for Ireland if it was re- quired—that was to say, they gave the house to understand that they had decided at that time to bring in a bill. The government had outdone so; the right hon. gentleman who had just sat down had declared to the house that they were incapable of doing so. (Hear, hear.) Therefore he said the house had been played with and had not been honestly dealt with. (Hear bear, and " question.") .It was strange, he remarked, very strange that a bill to make people sober should come from the Conservatives. It was something fresh. (Hear, hear.) The Conservative party had been held to- gether in the past bY nothing but beer. ("No, no," and hear, hear.) The Prime Minister might have gone further with the bill, as instead of opening public houses for two hours on Sunday the Opposition were prepared to say that the publicans should have a full day's rest. (Hear, bear.) They should also pass a bill, not only to close public- houses but to make it impossible for any gentleman to dis- graceshops and their makestreets, ai impossible nt nhaeayib werele f n r disgraced gentlemen to now,b withome out of. the proceeds. (Hear, hear.) Without question, the time had arrived for doing something for Ireland. He asked whatever bill had the Government brought in that had for its object the elevation of the people? A bill for Ireland had never entered their brain yet. ("Oh," and claaers.) He supported the amendment. •The member for CARDIFF rose to support the amendment --(hear, hear)—because it was agreed by an alteration in the Queen's speech that it would be necessary immediately after the passing of the coercion bill to con- sider whether it was necessary that certain laws should be altered which regulated the ownership of land and the relations between landlord and tenant. No such reme- dial legislation had yet been offered to the hese. They SIW no disposition on the part of the government to offer them such legislation—(hear, bear)—and, therefore he for one was distinctly of opinion that the government Was un- I worthy of the confidence of the house. (Cheers.) He roceeded to state briefly the course which he thought should be taken in order that the people of Ireland should be able to live in their own country in independence and in 'comfort. The past history of Ireland was known to all. rile present history of Ireland was like the past, except ! that at the present moment all its ordinary evils were 1 ex- • • Minted in perhaps a more ageravated form than they bad been at any previous period. There prevailed amongst three- 'fourths of the people of Ireland a distrust and total un belief in the honesty and integrity of English role. Thep - might be good grounds for that ill-feeling, but that it existed

'he did not think anyone would attempt to deny. The first step 'to be taken was to remove this feeling, and in " order, to do so he thought some great measure ' should be offered to the people of Irelandwhich would act ass complete demonstration to them that in future, wise, generous, new, and honest legislation shotild take place, and that equal administration and government measures for Ire- land should be meted out to them with the other parts of her Majesty's empire. (Hear, hear.) He suggested that the government should lend money to enable the farmers to purchase their farms in order that there might become a peasant proprietary in Ireland which would do away with many of the absentee landlords. Justice demanded that the people of any cenntry should become the possessors of the land which they cultivated, and the only objection he saw to the passing of such a measure was the existence of the House of Lords. (Hear, hear.) The member for BIRKENHEAD supported the bill, and criticised the speeeh of the right hon. member for Drogheda. The member for WEsruuArtr said not a word had fallen from the lips of the government in defence of the policy they had pursued. (Hear, heir.) As to the bill before the house he would be disposed to accept it with some suspicion, because it came from a quarter that had been closely allied with the drink- ing customs of the country. He proceeded to ask was the government that night worthy of the support of hon. mem- bers. ("No.") By their vacilating policy they had betrayed the confidence of the house. (Hear, hear.) They had not brought anything forward that was worthy of the confidence of hon. members. The house was formed for political education, and' when the originators brought it forward they considered it would be the means of edticating at least the government side of the house. (Laughter.) But the government had failed in the duty reposed in then In not performing their share of the work, and he therefore should vote for the amendment. The SPEAKER then called upon • the Prime Minister to , reply, when 4 The Ho mu SECRETARY moved the adjournment of the debate, amid cries of "No, have it out." ' The motion was then put to the house, when the Speaker said the " noes " had it, but the Premier challenged a I' division.

The house divided with the following result)—For the adjournment, 79; against 85. (Opposition cheers.) The Premier was again called upon to reply, but The HOME SECRETARY again rose and was met with loud cries of "chair," "chair," and " obktruction." He moved the adjournment of the House. The FOREIGN SECRETARY seconded the motion, and pro- ceeded, amid signs of impatience, to explain the propriety of lan adjournment. In the course of his speech, he said that he was afraid If they bad to wind up with a temperance sub- ject there would not be much jollity about it, a statement that was greeted with prolonged cries of "Oh," "their own measure,' and ironical cheers. The right hon. gentleman was about to proceed farther, when he was met with cries of chair." which caused the Speiker to rebuke the bon. 'members, and to ask if they subposed the chair did not know what it was doing. The member for BURY Sr. Enmrtrns supported the motion as things had been said which membersought to have the opportunity of replying to. The motion was put to the House, and the Speaker said the "noes " had it. (Opposition Cheers.) ' The Pattron then replied to the arguments adduced by the speakers against the bill, and referring to the amendment "the meaning of •which he had not yet been able to dia., cover," adverted to a letter, which bad appeared in th 4 Warrington Examiner, which, he said, expressed the views of one of the right hon. members opposite on the lard question. The LEADER of the 01%4)1111PN rose to ask if the right hon. gentleman attributed the authorship of that letter to I him. He could inform the Premier that whatever speech he delivered, or whatever letter he wrote, would appear in full with his name attached in another paper, which he named. (Loud laughter, and cries of " Boycotted.") The PREMIER went on to say that he was convinced no measure could be satisfactory which was not based upon a right principle. He Maintained that in Ireland there was a huge conspiracy at work, the object of which was to destroy the supremacy of the Queen; and which aimed at the disin- tegration of the empire. (Cheers.) He hoped the Land Bill woald improve the relations between landlord and tenant, and that it would be based upon right principles and regard the rights of property. Helloped the bill would be a good act, which would perpetuate the memory of a great statesman, who however much they might differ from him every one of them must hold in high esteem. (Cheers.) The house then divided on the amendment, when there voted in favour of it 89, against eV (Loud OppositiOn cheers.) • The PRIME MINISTER: Sir, it is necessary that t should now annound to the house that, having been defeated by a vote of the ,house, it will be necessary that we should hand our resignation to Her Majesty. (Hear, and laughter.) I ' may state for the information of the house that I shall re- commend Her Majesty, without any delay, to send for my right hon. friend the member for Stroud—(laughter)—who, I am quite sure, will not shirk the responsibility which he has brought upon himself. (Hear, hear.) I can only tell the right bon. gentleman that he will not find it any more a bed of roses than he did last time, but that possibly he may find more bills in the pigeon-holes than we did. (Laughter and cheers.) The SPEAKER: In consequence of the amendment having been carried, the original bill is thrown out. (Cheers, and a voice: "So Is the Government.") The house adjourned about eleven o'clock.

div.p: LITER ARI CURIOSITIES. A gentleman lately advertised as follows:— "Upwards of twenty thousand head of live stock to be dis- posed of with an unlimited right of pasturage." It turned out that the advertiser had several hives of bees which he wished to sell.
LONDON CORTIESPONDFNCE.

The earliest capture under the new protection rules of the House of Commons has been rather a comical one—a well- dressed man was observed hastily entering the lobby with a black bag. He was stopped, and the bag examined, when it turned out that he was clerk to Mr. Donald Currie, and had brought down nothing more explosive than papers re- lating to that gentleman's private business. The annual report of the Registrar will be forthcoming in about a month, and for the first time it will contain a feature of unusual interest. Each month will be divided into certain periods, and the prevalence of every disease will be shown for each of these periods, according as it exceeds or falls below the average of the past forty years. The ad- vantage of this series of tables is obvious, as it will be possible by means of it for even the unprofessional layman to tell in what month of the year each disease is most dangerous. It is but little known that matrimony, an expensive luxury at all times, is rendered more so in this country by a ; tax on wedding-rings. The duty is 17s. an ounce, and the revenue derived therefrom is about £20,000 per annum. The fashion of wearing very thick wedding-rings has greatly in- creased the revenue of late years —viz., from £6,000 to £20,000. Foreigners may well laugh at our callirg our. selves a Free Trade nation. In no other country in the world is a wedding-ring taxed. The news of the settlement with the Boers has been received with only a moderate degree of satisfaction. I be- lieve that the Tory party intend to challenge the policy of the Government, and it is probable, therefore, that we shall have a second vote of censure proposed on the Ministry a few days after the Candahar debate. There will be a double appeal. in Mr. Bradlaugh's case. It will be remembered that Mr. Justice Mathew decided not merely that Mr. Bradlaugh could not affirm, but that he might take the oath. While Mr. Bradlaugh has appealed against that part of the decision relating to affirmation, his opponent has also given notice of an appeal against that part of the decision which relates to taking the oath. I had a long talk with an .Africander, a member of the

Natal Legislative, who has lived 27 years in the colony, and is a fair and able representative of the views of the English colonist. He was under the gallery when the terms of peace were announced, and takes the gloomiest views of the result. He declares that the majority of the population of the Transvaal are loyal to the Ezglish rule, and that they have been " commandered " into the war by the energy of a few ambitious men. He prophesies that as soon as the Boers get affairs into their own hands they will make life unbearable to any English settler, and will give much trouble to their neighbours by bringing about wars with the native races. What he wanted was to see the revolt put down with a strong hand, and the Boers reduced to the condition of a subject race. All this was to be done by the English at their expense w"Ir"m" " This is the old story over again, which we may read in the Cape newspapers, and which is telegraphed to some of our journals by colonist correspondents. The highest notion the Cape colonists have of British colonial policy is that ' Imperial forces should be engaged to repress natives and foreigners, and leave the English settlers to make their fortunes in peace. The fate of Sir Frederick Roberts is commented upon in •various tones, according to whether the Speaker is his friend or otherwise. He will arrive in time to find the war over, and will not have the satisfaction, which Sir Garnet Wolse- ley enjoyed, of assisting in the terms of peace. These have been concluded by the direction of Sir Evelyn Wood, and everyone is glad to know that the gallant soldier who seemed to have lost his opportunity in one direction has found it in another.

. The annual report of the Inspector-General of Recruiting gives the following as the number of recruits who joined the different arms of the service during the year 1880:—House- bold Cavalry 128. Cavalry of the Line 1897, Royal Artil- lery 3759, Royal Engineers 442, Foot Guards 956, Infantry of the Line 17,581, Colonial Corps 209, A. S. Corps 305, A. IL Corps 345, making a total of 26,622. The only branch of the service which is below its establishment is the artillery.

TRADE OUTRAGE. An abominable trade outrage has been committ, 1 at Wal- lasey, on the Mersey. The operative brickmakers are aggrieved at their masters having employed some men from Liverpool, anti on Sunday night two beds of prepared clay were largely sprinkled wilh needles and small nails. The employers have resolved to use all means to bring to justice the perpetrators of the outrage.

WARD AND Locit's UNIVERSAL Iwerittrron.—(London, Ward, Lock dt Co.) The fourth part of this excellent work opens with the seventh lesson in botany, the seventh in French grammar, geology., ancient history, English gram- mar, chemistry, and physical geography, 6zo. Music is also one of the subjects taught. The lessons are all of a high character, intendedto make the student master of the studies he sete.,cts.

11,Izaa's MID-MONTHL. Sornarer...—(London : Goubaud, & Son). This popular magaziae for this month contains in- teresting articles on dress, needlework, etiquette, &c., with the latest fashions for children and costumes. It is accom- paniedbya!diagram sheet and patterns for cutting the Nadeje costume, the Ashliegh:paletet, and the Aimee dress, and cut out paper patterrss of a blouse costume, for a little boy. Tins ILLUSTRATED HOUSEHOLD JOURNAL (London: Ward, Lock, and Co.).—This well-managed magazine of fashion, fiction, fact, And fancy, home management and social intercourse, art and literature, contains a series of im- portant, interesting, and instructive articles. The supple- ments, this month, are a large coloured fashion plate and a cut out paper pattern of a child's ulster. - -

BRETON'S GREAT BOOK OF Porrnx.--(London ; Ward, Lock and Co.—The fourth monthly part of this publication has been issued, and when complete will form a fine col- lection of nearly 2,000 of the best pieces in the English language. The sketches of the history of the poetry of our country and biographical notices of the poets are exceed- ingly interesting to all lovers o/ the divine art of poesy. No doubt this publication will be regarded as a boon by those who are unable to purchase large quantities of books. WORTHIES OF • TIER WORLD (London: Ward, Leclt and Co.)—We have before us the fifth part of this work, which is full of intense leterest. It deals with 'men of thought and men of action, with great poets, philosophers, warriors, statesmen, orators, divines, explorers, inventors, dm. The biographies are well and concisely writtea, and filled with picturesque incidents, making them very attractive. Our readers may have an idea of the scope of the work from the fact that the parts which have already been issued con- tain the lives of Raleigh, Schiller, Blirke,' Napoleon L, Johnson, Goldsmith, Gladstone, Beaconsfield, Luther, Chancer, Humboldt, Wellington, Nelson, Chatham, Bunpn, Shakespeare, Jrc.

EVERY MAN HIS OWN MECRANIC.—(London, Ward, i Lock and Co.) This work, the fourth monthly part of which has now been issued, is an illustrated guide for ama- teurs who desire to help themselves. In it full instructions are given how to become your own mechanic, or as the author says, "Mend your broken chairs and crippled furni- ture; put fresh panes of glass into your broken windows; do your own repairs as far as it is practicable, indoors and out of doers; look after your own locks and fastenings; make your own-garden plant and appliances; put up your own sheds, greenhouses, and garden buildings, and I will answer for it, that if you check what you save ow each job, you shall find yourself in pocket at the end of the year merely through resorting to self-help."

ST. HELENS POLICE COURT. --- Frey:var.—Before Messrs. W. and T. Pilkington. POVERTY AND THErr.—Sarah Armstrong, who had in her arms an infant six months old, was charged with stealing a pair of blankets, value 155., the property of Caroline Wel- ford, Peter-street, with whom the prisoner and her husband lodged, up till recently, for a month.—The prisoner's hus- band is a painter and grainer by trade, and obtained work at the shop of Mr. Maclean, but only for'a short "paiod. On the 15th March the blankets were missing, and soon after

prisoner and her husband left the town. 'They were appre- hended at Pi est..n on Wednesday.—Prisoner said that after her husband had finished with Mr. Maclean they were in great want, and they pawned the blankets, but not without the knowledge of the prosecutrix. Mr. Maclean had promised her husband a job in a week or so, but they went to Preston in. search of a job in the meantime, and were on their way back to St. Helens when they were apprehended. —Prisoner was sent to prison for a month.
MONDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Pennington, jun., and T.

Pilkington. THE "Steinmann " CASE.—Me. Swift said this was a casninwhich Mr. Parks, shopkeeper, was summoned by Mr. Hart, borough engineer' for adding a projection to his shop in Church-street. Mr. Riley was instructed to appear for the defendan4 and he (Mr. Swift) appeared for the Corpora- tion. and Mr. Riiey called upon him at the end of last week to see if he would consent to a further adjournment until next Monday, subjoct to the sanction of the Bench, and he (Mr. Swift) at once consented to this. It was a case of some importance between the parties, and he supposed his friend wished to get it up very carefully.—The Bench agreed to the . adjournment.

Doe} LICENSES : Ma. Smarr ALAlnflp.—Several people •were summoned for neglecting to take Out licenses for their dogs. George Mobberley, Parr, who was fitted 255. and costs for a similar offence in August last, was fined 255. and costs is each case, for neglecting to obtain licenses for his two dogs.—Peter Swift, who was fined £5 for using his dog in taking • game a short time ago, was fined 255. and costs for not having a license for the same dog.—Daniel Swift, Parr, was mulcted in a similar 'penalty.—Michael M'Govern, Langtree-street; Thomas Travis, John Cottam, Isaac Ramsdale, all residing in Park-road, Parr, Were fined 255. and costs.--Martha Mil- ler pleaded not guilty and said she had no dog at all. P.C. , Lindsey said he found a small terrier dog in defendant's kitchen in Park-road. Defendant told him the dog belonged to her son, who had brought it from Huyton, but she in- tended to take out a license to-morrow.--Defendant said she had nothing to pay with, as she was a widow, and was receiving .relief. The dog belonged to her little boy. Mr. Pennington: What age is he? Defendant He is only seven years old—(laughter)—and lives with his grandfather at Tarbock. He has taken it back with him. Fined 255. and costs.—Robert Marsh and Thomas Topping were each fined 4255. and costs. Mr. Swift: I am in some of these meet, and I am rather alarmed at the course your worships are taking. I almost think your worships cannot be aware that you can mitigate these penalties. Formerly you could no mitigate them below 255., but now you can mitigate them as much as you please. An inaudible conversation , here ensued between the magistrates, andthen Thomas John- son, Parr-street, was charged with a similar offence. De- , fended said it was a stray dog, and they did not in- tend to take out a license until they found the owner. De- fendant, however took out 'a license the same day as the policeman called. Richaid Houghton stepped into the box and said, about seven weeks ago he lost his dog, but found that Johrson had picked it up, and as be had taken out a license for it, he allowed him to keep it.—The Case was dis- missed.—Sarah Johnson was similarly charged, and although she "could not very well afford it" she sent for a license while the officer was in the house. Her boys had been out on strike, and when the policeman called they had not had a reckoning. The case was dismissed.—James Sheppard was fined ss. and costs.—Jonathan Tyrer, public-house keeper, Shaw-street, who said he had" neglected it," was fined ss. and coets.—Mattheve Callaghan, John Heaton, Riche* Dean, and William Lyon were each fined 55. and costs.—Francis France, manager of the St. Helens colleries, was fined 59, and costs, because "having been so busy lately on account of the strike," he had neglected to take out a license for his dog.—Charles John Young, curate of St Thomas Church, who was repre- sented by Mr. Swift, mid who was under the impression that the license held good from March to March, his last license being dated that month, was fined Sc. and costs ; and Stephen Pennington who had a dog which would not bark when anyone entered hie yard was fined 10s. and costs in respect of two dogs.--George Hoot, who did not appear, was fined 255. and costs, and John Birchall, who said that his wife had "left him without telling him she had not got a license" was mulcted in the same p.nalty. Birchall was said to be the keeper of three dogs.—George Webster, greengrocerl was fined ss. and costs and Thomas Charles Wilcock, provision dealer, who had taken out licenses for years, but had forgot this time," was fined ss. and costs in two cases.--John Sed- don, Who did not appear, was fined 255. and costs. Francis Mercer, John Mather, James Trantram, John Burrows, Mary Ann Beach;lohn Richardson, Edward Marsh, Frances Mary West (for whom Dr. Davidson, solicitor, appeared> were tnulcted in the penalty of 58. and costs.—John Patrick Meams was summoned for having, without a license, a:dog which had been sent to him and which ran away up till two doys before thepfficer visited the house, but the case was dismissed. Mr. Swift appeared in this case. Scum. ATTENDANCE CAsss.—Meesrs. Bamford and Dut- ton prosecuted 34 patents for neglecting to send their child- ren to school. One boy was sent to the Industrial school, and two to the Boys' Refuge- at 'Liverpool, the rest being fined in the usual penalty of &L end costs. womplet 7,0240,,8„.7mary Tyre!. of Eccleston, was sum- monefe by_Jane Travis, for using defamatory language towards here—Defeudant was bound over, in £lO and two sureties in 1.5 each, to keep the peace for three months. WEDNESDAY.—Before His Worship the Mayor. A YOUNG THIEF NICELY CAUGHT.—A lad. named Joseph Marsh, was charged with stealing a quantity of toffey and a black pudding, the property of Ann Adamson, Church- street, on Tuesday. It appeared that en the afternoon of the day in question the prisoner entered the shop, and was seen by Mrs. Adamson to take from the counter a black pudding and two sticks of toffey. No one was in the shop at the time, and the prisoner left, apparently with the conviction that be had not been seen. He was comfortably demolishing a por- tion of the sweets when he was set upon by prosecutrix's son. He, however, evaded capture, and ran some considerable dis- tistance along the streeet followed by his pursuer, who suc- ceeded eventually in capturing the prisoner. Prisoner was remanded until Friday. .41e. The Rev. S. F. Green, the inhibited rector of St. Pohn the Evangelist, Miles Platting.. .was arrested by the eheriff's officer on Saturday and conveyed to Lancaster Castle, under a writ for contempt of court. Indlgnatiea, meetings are being arranged, and it is probable that an earl.) epplication will be made to the Court of Queen's Bench fee the release ef the rev. gentleman. On Monday the rev gentleman was visited by several local clerg)men, including the vicar of Lancaster, in Lancaster Castle. Everything iequisite has been done to make the quarters of the rev. gentleman as comfortable as possible. He is in good spirits. and expects a speedy release. A meeting was held in Man- chester on Tuesday under the auspicea of the local Chordl of England Working Men's Society, at which resolution: condemning the imprisonment of the Rev. S. F. Green wen 'adopted.

PEASLEY CROSS (ST. HELENS) CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL

The annual tea meeting in connection with this church was held on Wednesday night in the school-room. After tea, to which a goodly number sat down, the meeting com- menced, the chair being occupied by Mr. R. Pilkington, who was supported by Revs. J. P. Ritchie and R. J. Ward, and Mr. J. Marsh. After singing and prayer The CHAIRMAN said he took that meeting as an indica- tion that Peasley Cross was going ahead vigorously, strongly, and thoroughly, and as an evidence that a down- right lively and friendly Christian spirit prevailed among them, and that good was being accomplished under the leadership of Mr. Ritchie. It showed , also that they had money to spend and to spare, or else how could they have purchased that very fine organ. (Cheers.) When he saw it he put it rather strongly, and said, "Well, they're extra- vagaut at Peasley Cross." The fact of it was there was a hidden gold mine somewhere, which would have to be drawn upon for something else besides music. Although they at Peasley Cross did not criticise their minister's ser- mons, he was going to criticise Mr. Richie to-night. They had had lately grand doings in St. Helens, ministers from all parts of Lancashire being there, and gave them what Mr. Ward called a "teetotal dinner," nothing to drink except St. Helens water. (Laughter.) He did not know that the speeches were any the worse fpr that; he thought perhaps they were better. They had sOme very good speeches, but he believed that Mr. Ritchie made, well, he would not say the best, but one of the very best speeches delivered. (Cheers.) He was very pleased and proud to hear him speak as he did. Mr. Ritchie had got a lot of humour and wit in him, but he fairly abounded with it that day. The ministers were really surprised, as they did not know what sort of a minister they could show them at Peasley Cross. The Rev. J. P. RITCHIE said the meeting was held some- what later than usual this year, and they all knew the reason why. About the usual time the miners' strike came on, and many of their people were so affected that they thought it would be inexpedient to have the meeting at that time, and he thought the wisdom of putting it off to a later period was now justified by the present gathering. (Cheers.) Almost ever since he came to St. Helens the times had been rather bad, but he hoped they were going to mend. It was appropriate to remember their mercies on such occasions, and they had very much to be thankful for as they had been able to dwell together in unity, and there was great concord and good feeling in connection with the congrega- tion so far as he knew. They had a number of men hold- ing office as deacons of whom any minister might be proud. In some places the-deacons gave the minister a great deal of trouble ; they sat upon him—(laughter)—and sometimes thrust deeds into his face, and asked him how he liked that. But their deacons did not do anything like that. Mr. Spurgeon said about deacons, "If you resist the devil he will fly from you, but if you resist the deacon he will fly at you." (Laughter.) He believed if Mr. Wenham were so enraged as to stick a knife into him he would do it for his good. The idea of getting an organ presented itself to the minds of some of • their people some time ago, but the times then would not admit of such an enterprise. However it was suggested that tables should be given at this anaual meeting towards the pur- chasing of an organ. It was thought they should not allow the matter to rest until the annual meeting, so they deter- mined to get it beforehand in order to have something to report at that meeting. Mr. Smith took the matter in hand, and they were enabled to purchase the organ for £5O; its cost price was £63, but they were enabled to buy it for the first-named sum by laying the money down at once. He was glad to see there were others amongst them not con- nected with their church or schools, and he was pleased to see Mr. McKechnie there—(cheers)--from the Presbyterians, and others from the Independent Chapel in Ormskirk-street. The apostle Paul said, "Without charity I have nothing," and they certainly had to make large demands on the charity of those outside. He felt very much gratified at the good feeling in all quarters. He met Mr. McKechnie in the street, and asked him if he could not get them a few mottoes, and he said, "Come down to our schoolroom, and get everything you see there," and almost went as far as to say "if you see any money about take that also." (Laughter.) The Wiles for the annual tea meeting had been given by good friends at the cost of 10s. a table, and he believed they I had got in that way over £lO, and more contributed in the way of gifts of tables. On occasions like that it behoved them to see what they had been trying to do. They had been trying to do a little good with the view of keeping alive religious sentiment. Mothers meeting had been carried on during the past winter by Mrs. Richard Pilkington, and he was very glad she kept her connection, and gave them such valuable help in connection with those meetings. He believed the mothers esteemed it a privilege to go there. The Dorcas Society was commenced in November with a tea meeting, to which the mothers were invited. That society had effected a great deal of good, and many poor families had been greatly helped. He did not know exactly how much, but a good sane had been converted into clothing, which was sold at half-price to the poor people. The teachers and scholars had manifested great interest in Sunday school work, and 15 out of 18 had passed the scholars' examination at St. Helens, one of them being third on the list of the middle division. Cottage meetings had been taken in band by Mrs. Hayes, who had considerable influence among the people at Parr, and she had made herself responsible for the finding of supplies: and the effect had been *o create a freshness of in- terest about those meetings at Parr. Some of the young, men had started cottage meetings in School-street. About his own work in connection with the chapel he did not come to speak; he would allow that to speak for itself. But he did hope that a better feeling was beginning to prevail. He believed they were getting more drawn together. He rather had the impression at first there was not a heartiness or sympathy per eading the people as a whole, but he thought they were now getting over that. In some places people would not go to a certain place of worship because some- body else who had offended them was in the 'habit of fre- quenting the name place. That feelirg was getting very much lessened. But, after all, nobody knew their own faults so well as themselves. At the time of the valentines, he got one telling that he made two collections on a Sunday, and representing that as the motive which got him into the pulpit to preach. The person who sent that may have had the impression that be was avaricious, but he quietly put the missive into the fire. Those who knew him best would give him credit for being above avari- cious feeling. He knew Mrs. Garner, who was the mother of them all—(laughter)—had a scheme about getting cups and saucers and tea urns, and after they had got cleaar they might appeal again. Mr. WErattoir, on being called upon, explained that he was not a deacon, as stated by Mr. Ritchie. In giving the financial position ot the church, he said they were £4O be- hind, but considering the bad times the contributions had been very good indeed. As to the school, he said the morn- ing attendance was net so good as formerly. They used to have in the morning one or two hundred, and now the average was 72; teachers' attendance, nearly 7. The afternoon attendance was 18, and the average attendance of scholars in the afternoon 209. Having spoken in praise- worthy terms of the young men's class, conducted by Mr. Gilchrist, he resumed his seat. The Rev. R. J. WARD spoke of the advantages which resulted in that church being connected with the mother church at St. Helens. He must confess that the Peasley Cross church was in some things iri advance of that at St. Helens; and he went on to say how pleased he was to find, when once preaching there, all the people repeating the Lord's prayer, which Mr. Yonge, of Warrington, had so much difficulty in introducing amongst "that most Radical congregation at Wycliffe." Mr. ALLEN made a stirring speech, in which he showed how thankful they ought to be in having difficulties to overcome, as it made them braver, harder, and truer. Mr. MARSH briefly addressed the meeting. During the evening the choir sang several beautiful selec- tions of music, and Mr. George Barton, jun., pleased every one by the way in which he sang "Love's request " and "My Arab steed."

ST. UELENS PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY. The weekly sitting of the House was resumed on Friday night, Dr. McNicoll, the speaker, in the chair. There was a small attendance of members. ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS. The member for MIDLOTHIAN being absent, an hon. mem- ber asked if it were true that Col. King-Harman had turned Conservative in consideration of being made a lord lieu- tenant by Lord Beaconsfield. The PRIME MINISTER said it seemed that the hon. mem- ber for Midlothian could not have a great desire to have the question answered, otherwise he would have been in his place. He was certainly aware that Mr. King-Harman was made lord lieutenant of Ireland by Lord Beaconsfield, but it had not been proved, although assertions had been made that he was a prominent Home Ruler, that the elevation was made on account of his Home Rule principles. The choice was made because he, Of all others, was most fitted in his county to occupy that position. The Conservative Government, when making any choice, only looked at the suitability of the man. RUNCORN POLICE COURT. SA.TUBDAY.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds (chairman) and Mr. John Brundrit. STEALING ROPE FROM THE OLD QUAY Doc.—Peter Jackson and Samuel Ellis, dock labourers, were charged with stealing 48Ibs of rope, the property of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, on the 10th inst. George Brown, a boatman, said that on the morning of the date mentioned, he saw the prisoner Jackson, and a man named Bushell (who was now awaiting his trial on a charge of stealing rope) on board a flat in the Old Quay dock. Bushell asked him (witness) for a knife so that he might cut the rope by which, the vessel was secured, and take it to the company's store- room. ,He refused to lend the knife, and told Bushell and Jackson they might get themselves into trouble. Some short time after, he met the prisoner Jackson, who asked him to say nothing about what had taken place.—A witness, named Amy Sadler, stated that on the 11th inst. she had a conversa- tion with the prisoner 'Jackson at Widnes, and he told her he had got into some ironble about some ropes, and was leav- ing Runcorn, and going to his wife's mother's at Ludlow, in Shropshire.—Mr. Dobson was called, and said be saw the prisoner Ellis, with Bushell, at the docks on the day of the robbery. Inspector Hollingsworth proved apprehending Jackson, on the 17th inst., at Ludlow.— Patrick Lavelle, aged 12, and son of Michael Thomas Lavelle, marine store stealer. Mersey-street, identified the rope produced as having beßn bought at his father's store from Bushell.—Superinten- dent Williamson said the evidence against Ellis was so slight, that he had to ask the Bench to discharge him.—The magistrates discharged Ellis, and committed the prisoner Jackson to gaol one month, with hard labour. MONDAY.—Before the Rev. E. H. P. Campbell (chairman), and Mr. W. Banks. POOR RATE SCIAMONsES : EXCUSING PAYMENT.—About twelve poor people Wended at the court, and on the applica- tion of Mr. Sutton,'assistant overseer, were excused from ' payment of poor rates on account of their poverty.

A HINT TO THE WIDNES CA.NAL BOATS' INSPECTOR.— A HARD CASE.—Robert Owen, owner of the canal boat, Camden, was summoned for using the vessel as a dwelling place without having it duly registered, on the 16th inst. Mr. W. Farrington, inspector, said he saw the boat on the Weaver canal, laden with manure, and in charge of a man named Thomas Gregson. It was unregistered.—Defendant made a defence similar to that set up by several other people who have been fined for like offences at this court, viz., that all arrangements had been made with the authority at Wid- nes, but, owing to the neglect of one of their officials, the necessary documents had not come to hand so that the boat could be registered.—The Chairman said that defendant would be fined in the lowest penalty, ss, and 15s costs, or, in default of payment, 14 days' imprisonment. George Brimelow, game- keeper, whose face indicated that he was given to 6' conceal- ing spirits about his person," was charged with assaulting his father-in-law, an old man named William Bradbury. Complainant, who is very deaf, wished to withdraw the case, but Superintendent Williamson, in answer to the Bench, said he was of opinion it ought to be heard.— Inspector Fl ollingworth said that on the previous Thursday night, the complainant came to the police station in a very excited state, and complained of the conduct of defendant, against whom he wwi sahse dg i ay given warrantin the t c ao bs ee issued.—The ui,eicl,...—v ST. hLe Leach, ch ha i, r foremanm antodefendant, pro- and , wsheocudtiodrsn;otsayp.ac.sHoliibtbaeryrt.worDd :e—fenYou ntsarweereeviedaecnhtlyfiadae drunken ruffian. Here is a heavy bill of costs against you. In June, 1874, you were brought up for similar brutal ill- treatment of your father-in-law. The old man has evidently been worked upon to spare you all he can; and I have no doubt you expected that you would be allowed to get off un- punished. We are not, however, inclined to let a ruffian like you go unpunished. Therefore we bind you over to keep the peace against your father-in-law for 12 months, yourself in £lO, and sureties in £5 each. In default of finding the sureties, you will be sent to gaol one month. INDECENT LANGDAGE.—AIice Prescott, a boatwoman, was fined ss, and lie. 6d. costs, or 14 days' imprisonment for making use of obscene language near the police station, on the 24th inst.—P.C. Bossons proved the case. STEALING TWOPENNY WORTH OF TIMBER.—Two lads named Henry Ackerley, and George Atherton were convicted of having stolen six feet of timber, value 2d., the property of the Bridgewater Trustees, on the 15th inst. Evidence • I 55., and 14s. 6d. costs, or, in default of payment, 14 days' imprisonment. The money was paid. TuunsDAY.—Before Messrs. W. Bankes (chairman) and Mr. H. Reynolds. A SHIP'S CAPTAIN CHARGED WITH NEGLECTING TO PAT Snsarme's WAGES.— Thomas Birmingham, captain of a brigantine, was summoned for non-payment of wages to several seamen, as follows :—Thomas Shoyam, £6 Is. Od ; Jacob Williams, £6 3s. 7d.; Thomas C. Davies, £6 3s. 11d. ; Oliver Broston, £5 ss. 7d.; Albert Browitt, £8 3s. Bd.; and Thomas Griffith, £l3 83.10(1. Mr. Burton appeared for the bolder of the principal shares in the vessel, who had com- menced an action against the remaining owners. The con- sequence of this was that on the previous night a warrant I had been issued, under which the Admiralty had taken pos- session of the vessel, so that nothing could be removed.—Mr. Ashton, magistrates' clerk, said that this proceeding could not effect the seaman's claim, and it would not be fair to keep the men at Runcorn. If the claims of the men were acknowledged as correct, a warrant for the various amounts ought to isssue. It was a question whether the men's wages would not hare had the precedence of any other claim, just the same as in the case of bankruptcy proceedings, where the salaries of servants had always the first call upon the estate.—Mr. Burton said in the case of a bankruptcy there was a statutory provision as to wages, but he thought there was not one in a similar case to the present. —Ultimately it was agreed that warrants should be issued for the payments of the various sums mentioned above, which included the usual allowance per day in the case of seamen detained at any port. CHARGE OF THEFT AGAINST A YOUTIL—A lad. named James Chandler, was charged with having, on the 7th ult., stolen two sacks, a singlet, 1± yards of flannel, and a knife, the property of an old man, named Frank Bothwell, the master of two narrow boats, named the John and William. The prosecutor stated that Re- the the date mentioned, the prisoner was employed on °IT he on de- boats, which was lying at Weston at the time, an. camped, after which the things were missed. A Snow OP °Bozo, AT ST. FIBLICNB. will be seen in referring to our advertisentent columns, a show of entire horses and brood mares will be held on Saturday, the 16th April, when several prizes will be offered.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Bibby (chairman), George Pilkington, F. IL Gossage, and Mr. W. L. Evans. RENEWAL OF THE THEATRICAL LICENCE TO THE VOLUN- TEER HALL.—Mr. W. H. Kershaw applied for a renewal of the theatrical licence to the Volunteer Hall during the next twelve months. The police offered no objection, and, en ithe neceesary sureties being forthcoming, the Bench ordered I the licence to be renewed. SCHOOL Arreernallot PnosiecuTtoNs.—The following were summoned by the Widnes School Board, for-whom Mr. Danby, clerk, appeared, for not sending their children to echool, and were each ordered to pay 6d. fine, and costs 4s. 6d. :—John O'Bishop, Adam areen, Peter McCaffery, Gregory McEvoy, John Murphy, John Riley, John West- head, Michael McLoughlin, Joseph Woods, John Bowyer, Hugh Nixon, Thomas Prescott, and Robert Rosy. The cases were proved by school attendance officers Davies, Joynson, and Woods. ORDERS TO MAINTAIN CHILDREN IN INDUSTRIAL' ScnooLs.—Samuel Fishwick, whose child was sent to the St. George's Indusirial School, Liverpool, about three weeks ago, on the application of the Widnes School Board, was ordered to pay 3s. per week towards the maintenance.— Thomas Stanton, who has seven children to support, and hoe one child in the school mentioned above, was ordered to pay Is. per week towards his maintenance. SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A WIFE.—John Nolan, a powerful- looking man, was charged, in custody, with assaulting his wife.—Complabaant, who appeared to be in poor health, said that on the 21st inst. the prisoner swung an axe round her head, called her several bad names, and, in the end, knocked her down and kicked her in the left side.—He was fined 20s. and Bs. 6d. costs, or, in default of payment, ordered to be imprisoned one month. A Derron ASSAULT CASE. Mrs. Kane, alias Honor McNulty, was summoned for assaulting a married woman named Ann Wakefield, of Ditton.—Complainant, who made a very rambling statement, alleged that on the 12th inst. the defendant came to her house, and, after abusing her, kicked her.—Defendant was fined 10s. and Ts. 61 costs. THE CASE OF STEALING HENS—Samuel Bishop, a dirty looking fellow, was brought up on remand from last week, charged with stealing four hens, one cock, and four ducks, the property of a man named Thompson (formerly of Church-street), on the 27th December, 1873.—The facts of the case have been already reported. On this occasion Richard Griffith'', who has suffered several months' imprison- ment for being concerned in the robbery, was called by the police, and said that though he had received the punish- ment he was innocent of the theft. He somewhat simply remarked that he pleaded guilty because he considered it was no use for a man to struggle against fate when he had once fallen into the hands of the police! He was then asked by the Inspector if the prisoner might have stolen the fowls and brought them into his (witness's) yard. He, of course, could not say that he might not have done.—The Chairman said although the case was one of strong sus- picion, there was not evidence sufficient to convict, and the prisoner, who denied all knowledge of the robbery, was dis- charged. STEALING LEAD.—A SHARP POLICE OFFlCER.—Patrick Mclntyre was charged with stealing 351bs. of scrap lead, the property of Messrs. Mathieson's on the previous Satur- day.—The Inspector of Police stated that the prisoner was employed by the prosecutors, and about half-past five on Saturday afternoon, P.C. Murray, whilst on duty at Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon and Co.'s chemical works, saw him going in the direction of Newtown, having under his arms a bag which was so heavy that he had to rest several times whilst going a short distance. This aroused th 3 officer's suspicions, and he went up to the prisoner and examined the bag, which contained the 351bs. of scrap lead. Mclntyre said he had found the lead amongst the waste at the prosecutors'.—P.C. Murray gave evidence as to the apprehension, and Mr. Louis Kilcross, manager to Mr. Mathieson, stated that the man had no right to take the lead away.—Prisoner pleaded guilty, and asked that the Bench would deal leniently with him, as he had a wife and family.—lle was committed to prison one month. CUTTING THE STRIP OF A RAILWAY CARRIAGE.—John Reddington, labourer, was charged with committing wilful damage to the amount of 2s. by cutting a strap belonging to a carriage of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany. Mr. Sansom, station master, Widnes, was present during the proceedings.—Henry Noble, guara, said that owing to a great deal of damage having been done to car- riages belonging to the company, instructions had been issued to the guards to keep a sharp look out on the condi- tion of the coaches at the various stopping places. He was in charge of the train from War- rington, arriving at Widnes on Saturday night at 9.36. At Fidler's Ferry, he looked at the strap in the the third-class carriage in which the defendant and another man were riding, and it was all right. When the train arrived at Whines, he found that the strap was miss- ing. He could not say what became of the second man, but he followed the prisoner, and charged him with stealing the strap, which he produced from his pocket, saying he had found it upon the carriage seat.—Prisoner made a similar statement to the Bench, and added that he was drunk at the time.—The Chairman said the magistrates considered the offence of which the defendant had been guilty most dis- graceful, and one which there was considerable difficulty in bringing home to any one. Defendant, who had been as good as caught in the act, would have to pay 40s. and costs, 7s. 6d., or be imprisoned one month. The money was paid. ALLEGED POCKET PICKING ON THE FAIR GROUND.—Jas. Stevens, shoemaker, and Mary Tierney, were brought up on remand from Monday, on a charge of stealing Ils. Bd. in money, and a pawn ticket, from the person of Bridget Ryan, on the market ground, upon the the previous Saturday night. There was also another charge against the prisoners of stealing a purse containing £3 14s. 61., and a number of pawn tickets, front the persou of Ellen Higgins, on the acme night, but this was not gone into.—Bridget Ryan said she was the wife of Martin Ryan, of 12, Charlotte-street, and on the 19th inst., about half-past seven, she was on the market ground, standing near a man who was selling earthenware. The female prisoner came up to her and commenced talking. Shortly after the female prisoner began rubbing against her, and the male prisoner was also standing near to her. When the prisoners came up to her, she had a purse and 118. Bd. in her pocket. She went home shortly alterwards, and then missed the money and the pawn tickets. She gave informa- tion to the police on Sunday afternoon, and identified the two prisoners, who were amongst several others, as being those who stood near her upon the fair ground.—Prisoners were remanded one week. THE NIGHT ADVENTURE OF A RUNCORN YOUNG MAN. --Catherine Carey, and Mary Clarke, two women, were charged with stealing from the person qf James Jones, of Church-street, Runcorn, Sc. Bd. in money, a silk handker- chief, a pair of sleeve links, a meerschaum pipe and case, on the previous Monday night, in Waterloo-road. The prosecutor who was dressed in a black cloth over- coat, said he lived at 85, Church-street, Runcorn, and was going to that town at about a quarter past eleven, on the previous Monday night, when be was met by the two prisoners, near the George Hotel. He was smoking the meerschaum pipe produced at the time, and the prisoner Mary Clarke aged him "if he would give her a smoke." He said he would, if she would stay where she was and smoke. She said she would and he lent her the pipe. At the time he had a silk handkercheief (produced) in his breast pocket, a pair of sleeve links in his left hand trousers pocket, fis. Bd. in money in his right hand trousers pocket, and the pipe case in his coat pocket. Whilst he was stand- ing there, the prisoner Carey asked him to go with her, but he refused. He next felt ionsething in his left trousers pocket, and he caught hold of what proved to be Mrs. Carey's hand, who had taken possession of the two sleeve links, which he immediately ..took from her, She told him that she only wanted to look at the links. He stood talking to them nearly ten minutes. He had been at Penny's beerhouse and left with a young man at eleven o'clock. He bad some beer, but he was not drunk, and knew what he was doing.l One of the peisoners said to the other, "We must go," and he then asked for his pipe back, but they went away without giving it him. Re followed them, and said "I want that pipe." The women went into a house in Nelson-street and fastened the door. When lie knocked a woman called out "Who is there ?" and he answered "A young man wants to speak to you." The female said, "Yon had better be going, or my husband will come out and shift you with his fist in your mouth." They positively ref used to open the door, and whilst standing there he found that the other articles had been stolen in addition to his money. He apprehended the prisoners, and on being charged, Clarke said," How could I steal them when 1:1 gave them to me ?" Carey made an unreportable reply. to the effect that she hoped the prosecutor might be stiffened. —Prisoners were each committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. George Pilkington. CHARGE GE STEALING COAL—Catherine Mitchell, a girl who had been apprehended on a charge of stealing coal from a wagon in the sid.ng of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.'s works on the previous afternoon, was remanded until Wednesday.

TEN SOIITIMORT GLACTANIIIM AND ICE MAC. TUBING Costrattr, LIMITHD.—The fourth annual meeting of shareholders was held on Monday, Mr. Edward Holding presiding. He stated that the directors had again to regret that they were not able to show a profit upon the year's wcalting, but at the same time they were able to point to a considerahle reduction in the cost of water, which hitherto had been a most expensive item. The Southport bank failure had thrown the directors behind a little in the way of improvements, for bad it not been for that they would now probably have had the electric light in the building The report and balance sheet were adopted.

INES 1

1-STNERS' AND OCCUPIERS' ASSOCIATION. On Monday afternoon, a meeting of the members of this association was held in the officers' room, at the Volunteer Hail, under the presidency of Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, for the purpose of considering what steps should be taken in rela- tion to the election of five members upon the Local Board and three upon the Prescot Board of Guardians. Amongst those present were the Rev. Father Finegan, Major Cross, Messrs. F. H. Gossage, J.P., Eustace Carey, Holbrook Gaskell, jun., J. L. Muspratt, J. W. Carlile, J. B. Gaskell, J. Knight, F. Liddell, J. Matthews, W. H. Kershaw, R. H. Davis, D. Hirst, Dr. O'Keeffe, David Forster, and G. I. J. Wells (secretary and treasurer). Mr. WELLS, after the passing of the minutes of the last meeting, stated that the accounts had been examined by the auditor (Mr. R. L. Jones), and there was a balance at the bank in favour of the association amounting to £l5 95. This year the election expenses showed a considerable de- crease when compared with those of the previous twelve months. The CHAIRMAN remarked that it waevery satisfactory to see the society was in such a good financial condition. He was also glad to hear that the election expenses were de- creasing. The next business was to consider the course to be adopted in relation to the vacancies upon the Local Board. The CHAIRMAN did not consider it desirable that the association should monopolise all the seats on the Board. There were no, five vacancies in the number of representa- tives, and all the retiring members were gentlemen who had been nominated by the association. Of course they were aware that in the case of Mr. Muspratt the vacancy was caused by retirement. He believed that their nominees had done their duty upon the Board to the best of their power, and with the supreme object of benefiting the ratepayers. The question they had to decide that afternoon was whether they would nominate five or a less number of candidates to take part in the ensuing election. No doubt it had come to the knowledge of the members that a considerable amount of dissatisfaction had been expressed outside as to the manner in which the business of the Local Board had been conducted. It was quite open to those ratepayers who were dissatisfied to elect men of their own choice, and it appeared nothing but right that they should have a voice upon the Board. Mr. J. L. MUSPRATT observed that he had been a member of the Local Board for a number of years, and he was quite , sure the retiring members were thoroughly worthy of the , confidence of the ratepayers. Mr. WELLS said he might state that Mr. Foster, one of those who retired from the Board, had positively declined re-election. Mr. Homsnoox GASEELL, jun., said there had been a good many charges brought against the members of the Board, and he thought the present election would be a very good opportunity of ascertaining the real feeling of the rate- payers upon the question. He proposed that the association should bring forward five candidates. The motion was seconded by Mr. Ilinsr, and agreed to. Messrs. Gossage, Carey, and Wells, who had intimated their willingness to accept re-election, were then formally nominated, on the motion of Mr. KNIGHT, seconded by the Rev. T. FINEGAN. Mr. Holbrook Gaskell nominated Mr. Thomas Handley, ironmonger, Widnes and Runcorn; Mr. W. H. Kershaw, Mr. John Houghton ; Major Cross, Mr. W. H. Kershaw; and Dr. O'Keeffe, Mr. David Forster. The ballot was then taken, and twelve votes were given for Mr. Handley and an equal number for Mr. Kershaw, five for Mr. Houghton, and four for Mr. David Forster. Mr. KERSHAW stated that he had not the slightest wish to become a member of the Board, and he must decline te stand.

Major CROSS was of opinion that Mr. Kershaw was so well posted on township matters, that if he would consent to stand, and was elected, his services would prove a great acquisition for the ratepayers. Other gentlemen spoke in the same strain; and, at length, Mr. Kershaw said that whilst he was a member of the Board be had done his best to serve the interests of the ratepayers, and, if elected, he should strive to pursue a similar course in the future. The next business under consideration was the nomination of guardians for the township. On the motion of Mr. J. L. MUSPRATT seconded by Mr. WELLS, thanks were accorded to Messrs. Carlile, Matthews and Gerard, for their services as guardians of the poor for the township of Widnes during the past year, and they were requested to stand for re-election. 'Mr. CARLILE, in acknowledging the resolution, said he should be unable during the forthcoming year to attend to the duties of guardian, as he had not the necessary time to do that and attend to the Local Board business. He thought some gentleman who was not a member of the Local Board should be nominated. The CHAIRMAN: De you really mean that, Mr. Carlile ? You are not playing the coy widow with us? (Laughter.) Mr. CARLILE: No, it is a question of time. Mr. KERSHAW proposed, and Mr. CARET seconded, that Mr. J. L. Muspratt be nominated as a guardian of the poor. Mr. MUSPRATT : I am not eligible. Major CROSS moved that the Rev. Thomas Finegamshould be nominated to fill the vacancy, as they were really in want of a man who could thoroughly represent the interests of the township on the Board of Guardians, and who knew the poor of the town well. Two years ago Mr. Finegan was a member of the Relief Committee, and he had a very clear recollection of the great service which he rendered to that body. Mr. Finegan would be about the very best man they could select to fill the office. Mr. CARLILR seconded the nomination, and Mr. Mu,- PRATT supported it. Father FINEGAN said it was really flattering to be nomin- ated as he had been, but he did not think that he had the necessary time. If he were sent to the Prescot Board he should do his duty, and be there ou every occasion when his presence was required. Major CROSS remarked that he was speaking the wish of manufacturers when he said that they would be glad to see Father Finegan on the Board of Guardians. Was It not a fact that most of the poor of Widnes belonged to the congre- gations which attended on the ministry of Father Finegan and Father Clarke? Mr. WELLS: Father Finegan's name has been mentioned as a Guardian, and I feel sure it would give great satisfac- tion if he would consent to be nominated. Father FINEGAN : I would rather you had nominated another gentleman, but I most sincerely thank you for the honour. The propositiodwas then carried.
