THE ST. HELENS AND WIDNES TRADES. JUDGMENT OF THE RAILWAY COMMISSION. On Wednesday morning, at Westminster, the Railway Commissioners, Sir Frederick Peel, Mr. Price, and Mr. A. E. Millar, assembled for the purpose of delivering judgment in this matter. The application was made by the Tharsis Sulphur and Copper Company, Tinto and Company, and Mason and Co., importers of ore; Taylor, Cameron, and Co., Strong, Reed, and Co.. and George and Co., owners of steamers conveying ore; and Campbell and Son, at St. Helens, and James Muspratt and Sons and John Hutchinson and Co., at Widnes, manufacturers of the ore, occupying works adjacent to the London and North-Western Railway Company's line. The various grounds of the complaint and facts of the case are set forth in the judgment. Mr. Webster, Q.C., and Mr. Ffrench, appeared for the appellants; the Solicitor-General, Mr. Littler, Q.C., and Mr. Moon, were for the London and North-Western Railway Company. Sir Frederick Peel, in giving judgment, said that this was an application under the second section of the Traffic Act, 11854, complaining of the London and North-Western Rail- way Company for not affording, according to its powers, reasonable facilities for the carriage of traffic from Garston Dock to St. Helens and Widnes. The traffic was pyrites, and the applicants were either importers or consumers oi ore, or owners of the vessels in which it was carried. It was the duty of the respondents to transfer the ore into the wag- gons in which the ore was sent forward, and a supply of waggons on hand was daily required at the docks to prevent the detention of the ships and demurrage claims, and to keep the factories at work where the ore was consnmed. For several months previous to the application being made there was a great scarcity of waggons at the docks, and the com- missioners were asked to decide that one of those facilities which the railway company was bound to afford was to pro-1 vide under the circumstances of this case sufficient waggons for the ore, and to take care that the loading' or receiving I of the ore was not delayed for want of waggons. By thel Act for transferring the undertaking of the St. Helens Rail- way to the London and North-Western Railway Company' the latter company, when requested so to do by persons keeping works adjacent to and having sidings connected with the railway thereby transferred, was at all reasonable times and with all due diligence to provide waggons suffi- cient and proper for the conveyance of traffics passing exclu- sively over the lines of railway thereby transferred, except- ing coal, slack, and refuse material. The duty cast upon the railway company by this section was limited to goods where there was a request for waggons to proceed over any particular lines of the railway, but when the duty did arise it determined what was a reasonable facility within the meaning of the Traffic Act as effectively as if it were a duty of a more general kind. The special obli- gation in this case upon thd railway company was the more incumbent upon them, because it was one of the terms upon which the St. Helens Railway- was transferred to them, and if the company nealecits obligation to find waggons it was answerable under Traffic Act. It Ms said that the ore from Garston Dock did not pass exclusively over the respondents' railway, arn(d the e he therefore that the respondents' liability was to be rn?astte Ts solely eel ye commissioners ses iAo nc et ro: wleBrse4O, f ionpdienpi opinion nn d t theiy of th treaffi e special e Act,between the old or new dock at Garston and Widnes, St. Helens, s, St Helens Col the lines of railway transferred from the I other places on the same railway passed exclusively over chiefly to application referred pany, within the meaning of section 1 of *the St. Helen' Transfer Act of 1864. to the traffic for which waggons were requ.sted on th.r terms of the section, and it alleged that the respondents had not at all reasonable times and with all due diligence pro- proper and sufficient for its conveyance. It ded:waggons ' vi

appears that ships with ore in dock were berthed and dis- charged by the railway company, and it was said as to many of the ships that more than a reasonable time elapsed be- tween their coming into dock and their unloading being finished. This was attributable for the most part to the work of unloading being retarded by the want of wae•o•ons • The words "no waggons" frequently occurred in the dock- master's account of the work done by each crane in the docks. It was quite clear from the evidence that the com- plaints that the ore could not be got from the ships nor de- livered to the factories for want ef waggons were well founded. The delays and questions as to time to be allowed after a ship was in dock or in berth before demurrage made shipowners reluctant to charter their ships for voyages to Garston. The main facts were nncontradicted by the re- spondents, as to some at least that bore date between the end end of September, 1879, and the end of March, 1880. But it was represented on their part, by way of excuse and explanation, that the state of things at that period were exceptional—that a renewal of trade, which commenced about September, 1879, caused their traffic to increase faster than they could find means to convey it, and that in par- ticular the requests for railway stock were so numerous that they had not enough stock for all in full, but that the whole of their general stock was put in circulation and dis- tributed equally as far as possible and in augmentation of it at once, and that they had now 2,000 waggons more than they had then. The Railway Commissioners were of opinion that the respondents had not now facilites according to their statutory obligations. It was not enough, having re- gard to those obligations, te distribute waggons equally as far as possible. They thought, as to the traffic in question, that the respondents' duty in respect of providing waggons, went beyond their general duty in that respect. They were required at all reasonable times, and with all due diligence, to provide waggons proper and sufficient for the conveyance of such traffic and waggons for the service on the St. Helens line, which might be demanded even in circumstances which would excuse a deficient supply in the case of other lines. The Railway Commissioners were of opinion that the com- plaints had been proved as to waggons for the carriage of ore from Garston, and that as to ore similarly circum- stanced in future it was their -duty to enjoin the respon- dents to afford all reasonable facilities for the receiving, forwarding, and delivering of it. With regard to the alleged undue preference in respect of berthing and docking ships from Havre, the commissioners considered that the ground of complaint had failed. The costs of the application must be paid by the respondents, except so far 29 they had been increased by this last complaint.

WIDNES SPA )0L BOARD The monthly meeting was held at the offices, Victoria- road, on Thursday. Mr. T. Sutton Timmis presided, and there were also present the Rev. Fathers Finegan and Clarke, Messrs. Taylor, H. Davis. Shaw, Bradshaw, and G. H. Danby (chairman). Mr. Davis, the new member, on taking his seat, tendered his thanks to the Board for the honour they had done him in electing him. He added that he hoped he would be of good service. The CHAIRMAN gave Mr. Davis a beady welcome. He remarked that he was sure they were all glad to see him, and it gave them great satisfaction to know that he accepted tne nomination. In saying this, he was confident he was speak- ing the unanimous sentiments of all the members of the Board. (Applause.) DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTER. This committee reported that during the month of IF the number of cases summoned before them had been —applications for payment of fees 171, and for contraven- tion of Education Act 238-409. Fees were recommended to be paid in 168 cases, 2 were refused and 1 adjourifed for further inquiries. The number of prosecutions before the magistrates was 5, and a conviction was obtained in each case. It was recommended that Mr. R. Holden Davis be appointed a member of the District Education Committee, in the place of Mr. W. H. Price, resigned. The report was adopted. ASSISTANT TEACHERS' SALARIES.—A. "REFLECTION ON TER

cousurrEn." The minutes of the School Management Committee in- cluded the following recommendations :—From the West Bank Managers—that Miss Beata A. Hughes (vice A. A. Barnes) be appointed assistant mistress in the senior girls' de- partment, at a salary of £35 per annum, rising by £5 annually to £55. The School Management Committee recommended that the salaries payable to assistant teachers be rescinded, and the following substituted, viz. :—Assistant teachers :—Boys: Uncertificated, not exceeding £75 per annum, rising by £5 annually to £lOO, subject to favourable reports from managers; uncertiticated, £45, rising by £5 annually to £7O. Girls, juniors, and infants: certificated, £5O, rising by £5 annually to £7O; uncertificated,£3s,rising by £5 annually to £55. Mr. TAYLOR, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said perhaps the Board would remember that some five years ago they made an attempt to fix the salary for teachers coming fresh into a school below the maximum salary fixed by the School Board, and he believed they got an appointment made in that way for the temporary schools at West Bank, but there was some dissatisfaction expressed by a teacher on finding that she was to come at a less salary than her prede- cessor. Five years ago there was a scarcity of teachers throughout the country, but at the same time he knew a particular case where a teacher who was in receipt of £35 per annum in Widnes left to go to a similar appointment under the Liverpool School Board at a salary of £3O. Al- though that Board were copying exactly the rules of the Liverpool School Board in respect to salaries, the Liver- pool Board had ado?ted a system of putting down any applicant's name, and if a vacancy occurred, of communica- ting with such applicant; and not being bound to give the maximum salary, they succeeded in that case in getting a teacher at £lO below the maximum, although when the Widnes Board tried it, even to the extent of £5, they were not successful. He knew there was an expression of opinion at the Board that it was a false economy, bui he was not convinced of that. In any appointment manufacturers I made they did not profess to give the maximum salary to new comers, but first of all gave them a salary to see whether they had the requisite ability; and then when the employers found they gave satisfaction they generally gave then an advance of salary according to their merits. He thought that was a sound system, both in regard to the commercial transactions and the Board's business. It was a system that he believed everybody adopted more or less in making their appointments; but when they came to those public matters, they found there was a scare about it. A special meeting of the managers had been held, and it was recommended that Miss B. A. Hughes be appointed. 116 then read the follow- ing letter from the West Bank managers:— lam requested to inform you that the applications fer assis- tant mistress are, in the opinion of the mistress, very inferior Indeed, and this they think may be attributed to the fact that the advertisement was issued for £35, which is a very low I figure for so important a position as the above, and will fail to secure the services of a person of ability and experience. There Is also an opinion that it is false economy on the part of the School Management Committee in lowering the salary to £35, as £5 is never lost with a thoroughly good assistant.—WM. CRABTREE, correspondent. He did not agree with the managers, and more than that he believed he had some knowledge of some of these managers, and he did not know any one of them who was likely to start anybody they engaged at the salary they might possibly get the work done for, but might even give a lower salary than they intended for the purpose of trying the servant they were engaging. His colleagues were both managers of schools in town, and it was more particularly at their ex- pressed wish that the matter was brought before the Board that day. The Clierniciat seconded the adoption of the minutes. Rev. T. FINEGAN said his testimony was that Mr. Taylor had faithfully represented the wish of the committee, and it was their unanimous opinion that they could make some alteration of this kind. He heartily co-operated with Mr. Taylor in his endeavours to reduce the expenditure on the teaching staff; and he certainly disapproved in the most emphatic manner of the letter that was before them, and of the assertion made by the managers of West Bank school in that letter. It was a public letter now, and it wise a reflec- tion upon the Management Committee. Of that be indivi- dually cared very little, but be thought it reflected a great deal upon Miss Hughes, who had been apprenticed. (Hear, hear.) It was upon this point that he wished to speak. He thought the managers represented Miss Hughes as being of inferior ability, because she was enagaged at £35. He thought it was the business of the committee to vindicate Miss Hughes's character. As far as his impression went he never saw a teacher apprenticed who bad better recommen- dations from her managers. The CHAIRMAN: It does not reflect upon Miss Hughes by name, but says the candidates as a lot. Mr. TAYLOR: She has been appointed for £35, and they say the applicants were very inferior indeed. The CHAIRMAN : Of course; she is lumped with the others. Mr. TAYLOR asked that the testimonials should be read, and this the clerk did. The CHAIRMAN : They are excellent testimonials. The Clumsier's remembered the occasion Mr. Taylor re- ferred to, and be dared say he was instrumental in defeating the proposal. (Hear, hear.) He thought the Board should remember that at that time there was a large num- ber of new School Boards formed' all over the country. There was a large demand for teachers—a demand greater than the supply, and the consequence was that good teachers could demand good salaries. It might be that since six or seven years ago a great number of teachers had been qualified, and there had not been that large increase in the number of schools since that time. Therefore there might be now a surplus of teaching power, and consequently the price would be lower. Did they know if it was so? Mr. BRADSHAW : It is so. There are very many indeed, and they are seeking to check the number. The CHAIRMAN supposed now the supply had overtaken the demand, and that might be a good and sufficient reason for reducing the salaries. However, he was quite sure it was not their policy, on the cue hand, to pay poor salaries— (hear, hear)—or to pay lower than the average. They wanted good teachers, and he was quite satisfied the effi- ciency of a school in a large measure depended upon the excellency of the teachers. On the other hand, he did not see why they should pay more than the market value. If efficient teachers could be got for £35 per annum, they had no right to pay more, and if the committee was satisfied that was so, he thought they were perfectly right in passing o lower scale. Mr. SHAW thought there could be no objection to th- passing of the minutes, but he was not quite sure that tb, committee had gone far enough. It struck him they migb make even greater changes than bad been contemplated by the recommendations of the committee that day. ,
